Which namespace does the fork publish under? persist took the bare persist. orthographic cannot: it is the markdown lane's one registered target, so api-doc/orthographic.json is already a committed regeneration proof owned by that lane, and the no-go hides the bare orthographic namespace from page enumeration. Forking under it would overwrite the proofs and render no page. So the authored target keeps the dotted orthographic.camera — the nakama.engine.defold shape — which takes over the retired ts-defold module name and leaves the route and import string byte-identical. The rule generalizes: when the retired module name already equals the publish namespace, fork onto it; only reach for a bare namespace when nothing else owns it. Which file do you copy? The ts-defold lane runs a type-mapping pass, so fixtures/ts-defold/orthographic.camera.d.ts says hash/url/vmath.vector3 while the codemodded output says Hash/Url/Vector3. persist's two forms were identical, so the template never had to choose. Copy the codemodded output — the authored lane emits its input verbatim, so forking the raw fixture would ship ts-defold's upstream type names and fail the declaration-validity gate. Forking the codemodded output makes the cutover a byte-for-byte no-op, which is what lets you prove the severance and any type correction as two separate diffs. orthographic then took that second diff: upstream documents follow as accepting one game object or a table of them, and the ts-defold binding typed only the singular target: Hash | Url. On a file the toolchain repo now owns, widening it to targets: Hash | Url | (Hash | Url)[] is a one-line edit plus a re-emit. It moves no recorded gate number — the fidelity comparison scores member names, the unknown token, parameter count, return void-ness, and optionality, and a rename plus a union widening touches none of them. The third diff is the signature correction, and unlike the second it does move name sets. The fork gained get_automatic_zoom and set_automatic_zoom (live API upstream defines and ts-defold never had), lost add_projector, get_projection_id and use_projector (deprecated stubs whose upstream body only error()s), and world_to_screen narrowed to the (camera_id, world) upstream actually reads — its third adjust_mode argument was silently ignored at runtime, so narrowing it is breaking on purpose. With nine ledger entries covering the withdrawn stubs and the three camera.script lifecycle hooks, the target reaches callableCoverage: 1. The markdown verdict is re-derived over the new export list and lands on the same no-go. The fourth diff is the field correction, which moves the constants half of that same list: MSG_SET_AUTOMATIC_ZOOM was declared from the pinned camera.lua, and MSG_USE_PROJECTION and ORTHOGRAPHIC_RENDER_SCRIPT_USED were deleted, upstream defining neither anywhere — reading either returned nil, so the deletion is breaking on paper only. The verdict is re-derived a second time and holds: the nineteen constants and five functions the README's API table does not cover are still the surface loss that drove it.

20164.content: Is your library a LuaLS target?

20167.content: Types the Lua stdlib already owns

20174.content: Some pure-Lua Defold libraries ship their own type information as inline LuaLS (---@) annotations rather than a .script_api. This toolchain prints TypeScript declarations for them from those annotations, so a consumer that declares the library gets autocomplete and tsc coverage with no hand-written .d.ts. resolve prints the declaration into the consumer's project from the library version it depends on, or from the sources pinned in library data. Adding such a library is data, not code: you add one entry to the luals list of the library's recipe.json, in its folder under the library data folder (the newest version-named folder under packages/library-types/data/; the library folder also holds the fetched sources under source/), run the three generation commands, check the emitted API-doc description, and commit the library's files and its artifacts. There is no pipeline source to touch — the same front-end that produces the druid types produces yours. This page is for library-type authors. Library data lives in the toolchain repo under packages/library-types/data/, so you add or change a library with a pull request there, not to defold-typescript/library-data. If you only want to use a vendored library in your own game, you need nothing here — just declare the dependency and run resolve. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root. Each tool reads and writes the library data under packages/library-types/data/ and writes its reports to api-doc/ and fidelity/ in packages/library-types/.

20175.content: Two facts decide it: It is plain Lua (installed via Defold's Fetch Libraries, no .script_api), and its source carries inline ---@ annotations — ---@class, ---@field, ---@param, ---@return on the public module. A hand-written library with no annotations is not a LuaLS target; those are maintained as hand-vendored .d.ts forks. A library whose annotations are sparse (near-zero fidelity coverage, see below) will emit a hollow surface and is not worth adding. The library's runtime require path (its moduleId) must not already be claimed by another library in library data — two front-ends emitting the same module would collide.

20176.content: Start with library add, which writes the folder below from the archive URL, with a starting luals entry and the sources it reads: Then edit recipe.json by hand: add typeRenames and externalTypes for the tokens the library's annotations leave unmapped, narrow sourceGlobs and ignore, and add an entry for each other module the library exposes. The tables below describe every field. Each library pins its own repository and tag — a LuaLS library ships no .d.ts, only annotations, and each lives in its own repo at its own release. Its folder is named for the repository: its <host>/<owner>/<repo>, lowercased, without .git (https://github.com/Insality/druid is github.com/insality/druid/). The folder pins the library once: | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | ------ | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | repo | yes | The GitHub repository URL, e.g. https://github.com/Insality/druid. | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | license | no | SPDX-style license id, surfaced by the library page's provenance block. Defaults to "". | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | refKind | no | "tag" or "commit" when upstream publishes no stable release (GitHub's latest release skips prereleases), so the docs page's adopt step names the pinned archive instead of linking a releases page. Omit it for a repo with releases. | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | --------------- | ----- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | reviewed.json | ref | yes | The exact release tag to pin. Resolve the newest stable tag (git ls-remote --tags <repo>) — never invent one. | Each generated module is one entry in recipe.json's luals list: | Field | Required | What it is | | ------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | sourceGlobs | yes | Globs selecting the .lua files to snapshot, relative to the repo root (e.g. ["druid//.lua"]). | | Field | Required | What it is | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | moduleId | yes | The library's runtime require path, dotted (e.g. druid.druid). This names the emitted declare module and scopes the module-function surface to <moduleId-as-path>.lua. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ----------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | namespace | yes | The artifact stem — the emitted files are fidelity/<namespace>.json and api-doc/<namespace>.json. The fetched sources sit under the library folder's source/<namespace>/. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | typeRenames | no | Map from a LuaLS type name to the TypeScript type text to emit (e.g. { "vector3": "Vector3" }). The value is emitted verbatim and may name an ambient global, including a dotted one like debug.FunctionInfo — it never contributes an import. Omit or {} when the library references no renamed types. | | Field | Required | What it is | | -------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | ignore | no | Globs excluded from sourceGlobs — tests, examples, editor widgets. Defaults to []. | | Field | Required | What it is | | --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | externalTypes | no | Map from a type name another target owns to { "module": "<its moduleId>", "name": "<its export>" } — see below. Omit when the library references no other library's types. | A missing required field fails loudly, naming the field, the offending entry and its recipe.json.

20177.content: A library that requires a second library annotates the borrowed type by its bare name (druid's ---@field on_click event). Left alone that token resolves to nothing local and lowers to unknown. Naming its owner in externalTypes instead makes the emitter write a real import at the top of the declare module block and resolve every use of the token to it: emits import type { event } from 'event.event';, types all 46 of druid's callback fields as event, and resolves the ---@class event.on_size_changed: event parent to a real extends. The import is type-only, so it binds no value and a library that exports a function of the same name (quest.event) still compiles. The key is the LuaLS token as written; module must be the owning target's moduleId exactly, and name its exported type. A token whose local name would collide with one the library declares itself fails loudly rather than silently shadowing it. The consuming project must declare that upstream library too. resolve builds no inter-library dependency graph, so a project that lists druid alone gets druid.druid without event.event — the import then degrades to an error-any under the repo-wide skipLibCheck. Declare both; druid does not run without event.event at runtime either. quest and token import event from event.event the same way (quest also imports queue), so a project that lists either one declares defold-event beside it. Prefer externalTypes over a typeRenames entry pointing at an import(...) type: the api-doc lowering maps through the same context, so an inline import('event.event').event would render as the user-facing signature on the library's /api page, where externalTypes renders the clean event. A runtime require is not by itself a type dependency, so decide from the annotations rather than the requires. panthera opens panthera/panthera.lua with local tweener = require("tweener.tweener"), yet no annotation in its subtree names a tweener type — every easing is annotated string|constant. It therefore takes no externalTypes entry, and a project consuming panthera needs defold-tweener installed for it to run but not for its types to resolve — the inverse of druid, which needs event.event for both.

20178.content: Some tokens belong to no target at all — the ambient Lua standard library already declares them. log's ---@param debuginfo debuginfo names the table debug.getinfo() returns, which lua-types types as debug.FunctionInfo. That takes a typeRenames entry, not an externalTypes one: The emitted signature reads debuginfo: debug.FunctionInfo with no import line, and the log page renders that same dotted name — the way Vector3 and Opaque<"node"> already render there. The rule: a token another target owns takes externalTypes and gets an import; a token the ambient stdlib already declares takes a dotted typeRenames value and gets none. A library that declares the token itself wins over either, so a rename never shadows a real local declaration. Two naming rules keep such a local declaration from hiding the type a rename names, and both apply with no configuration. An alias that names itself in its own body means the type it shadows: ---@alias hash userdata|hash emits type hash = Opaque<"userdata"> | Hash, and every other hash in the library still names the local alias. A declaration named like a core or typeRenames value is declared with a trailing underscore: ---@alias Url url|string emits type Url = Url | string, the library's own Url references read Url, and an engine url still reads Url. Two declarations that land on one generated name, such as Url beside the library's own Url, fail the emit naming both. Where an upstream annotation restates a member it inherits from such a parent, and restates it incompatibly enough that the emitted redeclaration would not type-check, drop the restatement with an annotationOverrides field override — "fields": { "subscribe": { "drop": true } } — and let the member inherit. Like every override, a drop naming an absent field throws rather than passing silently. The second drop shape is a class-level @overload. The emitter lowers one onto the interface as a call signature, which is right whenever the class really is callable — event's EVENT_METATABLE and PROMISE_METATABLE each carry a real call. It is wrong where the @overload describes the module table while the interface types the instance: log reuses one table as both, but only the module table gets call, and get_logger returns an instance built on { index = M }, which Lua never treats as callable. Drop that signature with "callSignature": { "drop": true } on the interface. Same loud failure as the others: an override naming an interface that has no call signature throws. Some libraries bind a ---@class to a field of the module table instead of declaring a ---@field for it: token writes ---@class token.event.on_token_change: event directly above M.on_token_change = event.create(). The class becomes an interface, but nothing exports the value, so token.on_token_change would not exist in TypeScript. A moduleObject override names the module's class and each bound field with its class: Each field emits as export const on_token_change: token_event_on_token_change;, documented with its class's description, and the module's own class is no longer emitted as an empty interface. The override throws when the module class or a field's type is absent from the model, when the module class already declares the field (upstream added the ---@field, so delete the entry), when a module function has the same name, and when the parser already treats a different class as the module object. Other libraries assign constants to the module table with no annotation at all: live-unbundler writes M.MSG_ALL_LOADED = hash("all_loaded") and M.RES_BOTH = 3 at the top of its module file, so the lane exports neither. A moduleConstants override types each one with a LuaLS token and an optional doc line: Each entry emits as a documented export const MSG_ALL_LOADED: Hash; and appears on the /api page, and its token counts toward the fidelity report like any annotation. Only a column-0 M.NAME = ... on the table the module's own file returns (return M) counts as an assignment, as does the first target of M.DEBUG, M[1] = 1, "DEBUG"; an assignment on another table, such as Other.NAME = 1, does not. The override throws when the returned table never has the name assigned at column 0, when a module function has the same name, and when the module object's class already declares it as a field. A ---@meta file can describe a class's functions with dot syntax: ads-wrapper's ads_networks/ads_network.lua starts with ---@meta, puts ---@class ads_network on local ads_network = { NAME = "ads_network" }, and then annotates function ads_network.setup(params) and its siblings. When the tag is the file's first non-blank line, each such function becomes a method of ads_network declared with this: void (setup(this: void, params?: unknown | undefined): void;), because callers invoke it as network.setup(params), not network:setup(params). In any other file the same form stays a module function, since a runtime module may annotate its own table as a class and still export its functions. A dot function on another local table belongs to that table when the returned module re-exports it at column 0. flow's flow/flex.lua defines function Node.new(opts) on local Node = {}, assigns FL.Node = Node, and ends with return FL, so new is declared on export const Node: { "new"(this: void, ...): Node }, not as a top-level flex.new. Because the file also sets Node.index = Node and Node.new declares ---@return Flow.FlexNode, the Node interface extends Flow_FlexNode, and new plus every method annotated ---@return Flow.FlexNode self return Node, so flex.Node.new({ key: "root" }).set_width(960).calculate_layout(960, 640) keeps the chainable methods. A table exported under several fields is declared under each field. A field assigned more than once declares the table it is assigned last. Where an annotation types a parameter wrongly, a type token on a moduleFunctions parameter replaces it: ads-wrapper's queue.lua writes ---@param fn ads_callback, though run calls fn(network, callback, params), so the ads_wrapper.queue target retypes it: add then emits fn: (network: ads_network, callback: ads_callback, params?: LuaTable) => void. A parameter of interfaces.<name>.methods.<method>.params takes the same type key. Naming an absent function or parameter throws. "optional": true on interfaces.<name>.methods.<method> emits the method as name?(...), for a method the library checks for before it calls it. ads-wrapper's wrapper.lua guards the call with if network.request_idfa then, so the ads_wrapper targets mark ads_network.request_idfa optional, and a network without it still passes ads_wrapper.ads_wrapper.register_network.

20179.content: Run the three commands from the toolchain root, in order. Each iterates every LuaLS target in library data, so an unchanged entry re-emits byte-for-byte and only your new entry produces new files. --fetch reads the pinned tree, applies sourceGlobs minus ignore, and writes each selected .lua under <library>/source/<namespace>/, preserving tree shape. This is the only command that touches the network; everything after it reads those committed fixtures, so the pipeline is reproducible offline. --fidelity parses the fixtures and reports how much of the surface resolved to a known type (see below). resolve prints the .d.ts a consumer sees from these fixtures, or from the dependency's own archive. Interfaces and aliases come from the whole snapshot; the module's own functions come only from the moduleId file. --api-doc-out makes library check lower the same model, once its checks pass, to the JSON the /api page renders. A ---@deprecated before a ---@class, ---@alias, or a function declaration carries into both artifacts — as a JSDoc @deprecated in the .d.ts and as a Deprecated line on the /api page, with the tag's own text when it has any. A tag on a type still reaches only the .d.ts, since a type has no page heading of its own to carry the line. Only the strict ---@deprecated form is read; a spaced --- @deprecated is treated as prose, as it is for every other tag.

20180.content: fidelity/<namespace>.json tells you whether the emit is worth committing: coverage — the fraction of type tokens that resolved to a known type. Druid sits around 0.9; a healthy new library lands in the same range. Near-zero means the source is not meaningfully annotated — reconsider the target. unknownTokens — the distinct type names that fell back to unknown. A cross- library reference (another Insality module) shows up here until you name its owner in externalTypes, which resolves it; the LuaLS placeholders and a bare ... are not among them, because they declare no type and now lower to unknown without counting against coverage, and neither is a bare function, because it now lowers to the callable type (...args: any[]) => unknown. A rename that should have applied shows up as an unexpected entry — fix typeRenames and re-emit. undocumentedMembers — members with no annotation at all; informational. Each report's coverage is pinned by a committed floor, the module's entry in floors in the library's library.json, so a regeneration that lowers it fails the suite instead of quietly rewriting the report, and library check measures the module against the same floor. Regenerating never touches the floors; when you genuinely improve coverage, lock the win in with which raises each floor to the current coverage and can never lower one. A drop is therefore always a real regression to fix at the source, never a floor to edit down.

20181.content: After library check --api-doc-out, open api-doc/<namespace>.json and inspect info.description. It carries the description line on the library's main ---@class. When that class has no description line the value is empty (""), and the /api page renders with no description — the "every library page has a non-empty description" gate fails. Remediate by adding a namespace-keyed entry to <data folder>/library-descriptions.json — "<namespace>": "<one-line summary>", keyed by namespace. The site's fallback in api-surface-loader.ts reads it for LuaLS libraries (a ts-defold library keys its fallback on the upstream classification dir; a LuaLS library has none, so it keys on the namespace directly). druid needs nothing here — its ---@class druid is described, so it never reaches the fallback. decore is the worked example: its ---@class carries no description, its api-doc/decore.json info.description is "", and the committed "decore": "Defold ECS Data Manager" entry supplies the page description.

20182.content: Run library check over the library data. It runs the reader's checks, prints every module, and type-checks every module resolve prints under skipLibCheck: false, together with each library folder's usage/ examples, so a new target is compiled as soon as its recipe.json lists it; the dts-declaration-validity test runs the same check. Fidelity parity is gated per namespace. Then run the library tests: A brand-new library has no floor entry yet, and the floor gate fails until it gets one — fidelity-floor.ts --raise seeds it at the coverage you just measured. Commit the library's library.json with its floor, reviewed.json and recipe.json and the snapshotted source/<namespace>/ together. Both emitted report folders (fidelity/, api-doc/) are gitignored here and stay uncommitted.

20183.content: The druid entry is the reference shape: sourceGlobs snapshots the whole druid/ tree; ignore drops its tests and examples; moduleId druid.druid scopes the exported functions to druid/druid.lua while the interfaces merge from every file; typeRenames maps druid's vmath references onto the toolchain's branded Vector types; externalTypes hands druid's callback fields to the event library that owns them. From these fixtures, or from the druid archive a project depends on, resolve prints the declaration it materializes into a consuming project as druid.druid.

20184.content: A native or hybrid library that ships an extension .script_api (the same YAML format every Defold extension ships) has a third ingestion mode, distinct from the LuaLS front-end above: packages/cli/src/library/sync-script-api-types.ts, driven by the scriptApi list of a library's recipe.json. Instead of parsing ---@ annotations, it routes the committed .script_api snapshot through the shared ref-doc emitter — scriptApiToFixtureJson → generateModuleDeclaration, the exact path resolve-time extension typing uses — so one-level nested sub-namespaces (bridge.platform, bridge.achievements) survive into nested namespace blocks. The output is an importable module keyed by moduleId (declare module 'bridge.bridge'), matching the LuaLS library goldens, so the library imports under its pinned specifier; the declare global form stays the resolve emitter's, for extensions a project declares. Each entry names scriptApi (the path to the .script_api in the repo), moduleId, namespace, and the exact apiDoc / fidelity output paths; the library folder pins repo and ref as above. The generate arms mirror the LuaLS ones: The first migrated target is Playgama/bridge-defold (pinned v2.3.0), maintained entirely from its .script_api — its former ts-defold binding is gone. Three things are specific to a script_api target and worth knowing: Output paths are pinned explicitly and named for the single-segment namespace. Like the LuaLS libraries, a migrated script_api library is the sole maintainer of its namespace, so its goldens are api-doc/bridge.json and fidelity/bridge.json — not the dotted moduleId — which keeps the docs Libraries tree and the file layout uniform with druid. The require specifier is still the moduleId (declare module 'bridge.bridge'), so resolve prints it under that specifier. Fidelity mirrors the emitter, so an unmapped token counts against coverage. The report is computed over the ref-doc doc with the emitter's own type map: a token the emitter renders as unknown is counted in unknownFallbacks and listed in unknownTokens rather than hidden. A pipe-separated type: or a YAML list (type: [table, string]) is split into one token per alternative before that check, so bridge's string | nil returns resolve to string | undefined and bridge lands at coverage 1. A slot left with no token at all counts as one unknown fallback, listed as (untyped), so it cannot pass as covered. A parameter upstream calls omittable in prose only is declared, not inferred. The .script_api format cannot say that a middle parameter may be left out with the later ones shifting left, and upstream sometimes describes a trailing parameter as optional without marking it optional: true. A target lists either kind of slot under omittableSlots (element, slot, and the upstream evidence that allows it), and the emitted declaration carries two overloads, with and without it. The api-doc page and the fidelity report stay as upstream wrote them. A slot the fixture no longer has fails the emit, so the entry cannot go stale.

20190.content: How a stale pin is noticed

20193.content: The couplings a re-pin moves with it

20194.content: What a re-pin does not touch

20197.content: Every library whose types the toolchain ships is pinned to one upstream ref in one of five lane registries: the LuaLS, script_api and authored registries, with the fixtures their entries name, sit in the newest data folder, packages/library-types/data/<version>/, and the markdown and OpenAPI registries at the root of packages/library-types/ in a toolchain checkout. Upstream keeps moving; the pins do not. This page is what to do when one of them has fallen behind. Authoring LuaLS library types and Authoring forked library types cover adding a library. This page covers moving one that is already there, which is a different job: the generation commands are the easy half, and the couplings that move with the pin are the half that is not discoverable from the sync scripts. This page is for maintainers of the library data in the toolchain repo, changed by pull requests there. Consuming a library in your own project is resolve, and your project's declared dependency version is unrelated to the pin here. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root unless a step names another folder.

20198.content: The Library update workflow (the toolchain's .github/workflows/library-update.yml) runs library update over packages/library-types/data/ with the latest CLI, then opens one pull request per library it wrote, from the branch library-update/<library>. It runs daily, and when dispatched: A PR that moves a pin is titled update <library> to <ref>; one that only adds commits to a review is titled record <library> commits. A later run force-pushes the same branch and retitles its open PR, so a library never has two. A library that cannot be read upstream is named in the run's log, and fails the run once every other library has its PR. A run dispatched while another is going waits for it to finish.

20199.content: The workflow turns on auto-merge, so the PR merges once ci-done passes, only when both hold: the change is kept or added, or the PR only records commits; every file the PR touches is the library's reviewed.json or under its source/, and CI scopes it as library data. The second is read from the commit, not from what library update reported, so a file anything else wrote keeps the PR for a human. Every other PR stays open. A run turns off an open PR's auto-merge before it replaces the branch, and turns it on again only for the commit it read.

20200.content: The PR body names the change and the members upstream added, removed and changed. A changed PR whose three lists are all empty had no single review of the pinned commit to compare with, so read the diff under source/ instead. The library-check run on the PR says whether the library still fits: a module below its floor is named with the value it measured, and a usage/ proof that stops compiling is named by file and line. Fix the fork, floor or proof as the couplings a re-pin moves with it describe, on a branch of your own: the next run force-pushes library-update/<library> and drops any commit pushed to it. Once yours merges, the next run finds the library current and closes the bot's PR.

20201.content: follows in a library's library.json says what library update watches: tags in the pin's series, the default branch, or none. With none set, a library pinned to a commit follows its default branch and any other follows its tags. none holds a library, and no request is made for it. library-defold-persist and library-defold-rendy follow none because their whiteboxdev repos answer 404, which would fail every run; they hold no review, so resolve reports them unrecorded.

20202.content: The library update workflow runs daily, so a library that moved upstream gets one PR from library-update/<library>, refreshed on each run. The bot closes that PR, with a comment, once a run finds the library current or held, or no longer lists the library, as when a new data folder renames it. The bot files an issue titled library update cannot land <library> only when it cannot land a library: library update failed for it, or its PR's checks were red when the run started. The issue names the failure or links the PR, a later run edits it rather than filing a second, and the bot closes it, with a comment, once neither holds. A run reads the checks before it refreshes any PR, so an issue opens or closes up to one run after the checks finish. bun run upstream:library-check is a manual report that no workflow runs. It scans all five registries and reports, per upstream repo, whether the pin has fallen behind: Three things about the report are worth knowing before you act on it: The unit of work is the repo, not the module. britzl/defold-input backs ten authored modules and britzl/defold-orthographic is consumed by two lanes. One bump answers every dependent, so the check groups by repo + ref, counts the dependents, and lists them under --json. A commit-pinned repo is only actionable when the delta touches a path this repo reads. The registries already record which upstream files each target consumes, so a README-only commit on a pinned repo's default branch reports as behind-head without asking you to do anything. A pin that feeds only the fidelity comparison is marked internal. When every dependent is a markdown or OpenAPI target whose decision is not go, no user receives its output, so the report sets internal and the prose line ends in (internal); the bump needs no changelog bullet. It is still actionable: a stale spec hides upstream movement from the go/no-go comparison. The library update bot does not update these targets, so this report is the only place their drift shows. A repo the check could not read at all is reported as unknown and exits the command non-zero. That is deliberate: a renamed or deleted upstream must not look like "current". The check reads GitHub and Codeberg; a repo on any other host reports unknown. When an upstream moves, search the author's old repos for a pointer to the new home before withdrawing the library. Re-pointing means a new repo and a new ref together, because a moved repo often has rewritten history and the old commit no longer exists there.

20203.content: The registries only see libraries someone already added. <data folder>/asset-portal.json records every Defold Asset Portal entry, pinned to a defold/asset-portal commit, with the GitHub repo each entry names classified by what a dependency on it installs: The sync refuses to start without GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, because it makes about five API calls per entry. It follows renames, so repo is the canonical URL (the portal's britzl/extension-imgui is recorded as defold/extension-imgui). Each repo is read at its latest release, else its newest tag, else its default-branch head. Files count only inside the repo's game.project [library] include_dirs, since nothing else reaches a project that adds the dependency. Each entry's kind is the first row that matches: | kind | The repo at its pin | | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | no-source | is not readable on GitHub; reason is no-github-url or not-found | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | not-a-dependency | declares no include_dirs: a tool, sample or editor integration | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- | | script-api | ships a .script_api, which resolve already types | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | native-untyped | ships an ext.manifest without a .script_api | | kind | The repo at its pin | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | pure-lua-annotated | ships Lua, and one of up to four sampled files carries ---@ annotations | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ---------- | ---------------------------------- | | pure-lua | ships Lua with no annotated sample | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | no-lua-api | ships no Lua: shaders, materials, sounds or editor scripts only | bun run asset-portal:report joins the manifest against every lane registry and the defold org listing in defold-extensions.json, offline, and prints four answers: Tracked: entries whose repo a registry already pins, counted per lane. The portal lane counts the script-api entries that have reference pages. A tracked entry files here whatever its kind. Candidates: untracked entries of kind script-api, native-untyped, pure-lua-annotated or pure-lua that are not archived, not a fork, were pushed within 730 days of the sync, and carry no verdict. They are grouped by kind and ranked by stars, which only order the list and say nothing about quality. Declined: untracked entries with a recorded verdict, each with its reason. Nothing to type: untracked no-lua-api, not-a-dependency and no-source entries. A line between them counts the untracked entries with a Lua API that fail the maintenance rule. After a manifest sync, give every script-api candidate its reference pages: It converts each .script_api under the entry's include_dirs at the pin asset-portal.json recorded, writes the page list to <data folder>/asset-portal-script-api.json and one doc per page under asset-portal-script-api/api-doc/, and rebuilds that directory on every run. Those entries then count as tracked on the portal lane. A doc that fails to convert, a page key another page already holds, or a page key that is not one safe route and file name (ASCII letters, digits, , . and -, starting and ending with a letter, digit or , and not a Windows device name such as CON or NUL before its first .) stops the sync before it changes any file, instead of dropping the page. A page key names only the page's api-doc file: its address comes from the library's origin repo, as Library page addresses describes. A library that moved forge keeps a stale portal entry: the portal's Klaleus/library-defold-checkpoint is gone from GitHub, and the authored lane pins codeberg.org/Klaleus/defold-checkpoint. Map such an entry to the tracked repo in packages/library-types/asset-portal-aliases.json. The report refuses to run when an alias names an entry the manifest no longer lists, or a repo no registry pins. An entry whose pinned tree holds no runtime module a project would require, such as an editor script, an import tool or a project template, stays a candidate until someone looks. Record the decision in packages/library-types/asset-portal-verdicts.json: a map from entry id to one short reason naming what the tree holds instead. A verdict takes the entry off the candidate list for good, whatever its maintenance state. The report refuses to run when a verdict names an entry the manifest no longer lists, or an entry a registry pins directly or through an alias, since either verdict is stale. The weekly Library upstream check workflow (the toolchain's .github/workflows/library-upstream-check.yml) compares the portal head's entry ids with the manifest. When ids were added or removed, it opens one issue, titled Asset portal entries differ from asset-portal.json, that lists them and names the re-sync command. The title never changes, so later runs stay quiet while that issue is open. A changed entry under an unchanged id is not reported, because the portal rewrites release metadata every six hours.

20204.content: Four lanes fetch and regenerate. Run their commands from the toolchain root, in order, after editing the pinned ref: | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ----- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | LuaLS | the library folder's reviewed.json | bun run --cwd packages/library-types luals:fetch, then luals:fidelity, api-doc | | Lane | Pin | Commands | | -------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Markdown | markdown-targets.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-markdown-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --api-doc | | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | OpenAPI | openapi-targets.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-openapi-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --api-doc | | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ---------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | script_api | the library folder's reviewed.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-script-api-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --data packages/library-types/data, then bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc | A library folder sits in the newest version-named folder of packages/library-types/data/, named for its repository: its <host>/<owner>/<repo>, lowercased, without .git. --fetch is the only step that touches the network; everything after it reads the committed fixtures, so a regeneration is reproducible offline. No lane writes a declaration: resolve prints each target's types from its fixtures, so check them by printing them with bun test packages/cli/src/library from the toolchain root. Set GITHUB_TOKEN before fetching. The fetchers read it (sync-luals-types.ts and sync-library-types.ts both send it as a bearer token) and GitHub degrades unauthenticated API traffic — the git/trees calls behind --fetch and upstream:library-check can return 504 Gateway Timeout on every attempt while the rate-limit budget still shows requests remaining, so a 504 here is not evidence that the pin or the repo is wrong. The authored lane is the exception, and it is the one that surprises people. A library's forks have no --fetch and no fidelity pass. Their source/upstream/ snapshots are vendored by hand and their .d.ts is hand-written, so bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc is the only command they take. Refreshing an authored pin means: edit the ref in the library folder's reviewed.json; copy the upstream files named by upstreamLua into the library folder's source/upstream/… by hand (the path under it mirrors the upstream path); update the hand-written .d.ts for whatever the new upstream added or changed; re-run bun run --cwd packages/library-types parity and bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc.

20205.content: None of these are visible from the sync scripts, and each of them reds ci if you skip it. The committed floor. floors in the library's library.json holds a per-module measurement the gates and library check assert against. New upstream surface changes the measurement, so the floor entry moves with the pin — raise a generated module's ratio with bun run --cwd packages/library-types fidelity:floor, and edit a fork's or native extension's { callable, field } pair by hand. The parity reports. authored-parity-floor.test.ts checks each committed report under packages/library-types/fidelity/authored/ and fidelity/native/ against a fresh measurement of the vendored copy. After re-vendoring, re-run bun run --cwd packages/library-types parity, review the coverage change, and commit the reports in the same commit. An upstream change that moves no number leaves the reports as they are. The provenance assertions. The toolchain's api-surface-loader.test.ts reads the pin back out of the emitted API-doc metadata and asserts it exactly — for druid, meta.commit is the ref in druid/reviewed.json and meta.sourceUrl is https://github.com/Insality/druid/tree/<ref>. A bump moves both, and they are in a different package from the pin you edited. The pin kind. refKind in the library's library.json says whether the pin is a release, a tag or a commit, and the docs page's adopt step follows it. It moves with the pin: api-surface-loader.test.ts reds when the asset-portal register records another kind at the same ref. The pin-refresh record. packages/library-types/pin-refresh.json states which members a bump added and removed, one entry per refresh, each tagged with the lane it belongs to (luals, script-api, or openapi). packages/cli/src/library/pin-refresh.test.ts checks every name it states against the surface that lane's own parser yields for the committed fixtures — buildTargetModel, committedScriptApiDoc, or parseOpenApi. Regenerating the fixtures without updating the record reds ci, so derive the new entry by diffing the old and new member names rather than from upstream release notes. A second key, deliberatelyUnmoved, records a pin you examined and chose to leave alone, and is guarded on its ref alone — so a note left standing after that pin later moves also reds. The guard deliberately does not check that the record is complete, nor its changedMembers and notes, which are prose. The compile-only surface proofs. The .test-d.ts files under each library folder's usage/ assert the emitted .d.ts by assigning from it, and pin the absence of non-public members with @ts-expect-error. A bump breaks them in both directions: a member that left the public surface fails the assignment, and a member upstream stopped marking @field private or @local makes its expect-error directive unused (TS2578). The second is the easy one to misread — check the old and new fixture annotations before assuming the emitter regressed, because dropping a private marker upstream is a real surface change and the declaration is then correct to emit. The generated docs artifacts. packages/docs/llms.txt, packages/docs/llms-full.txt, and the docs-site search and symbol indexes are committed, not built on demand. Regenerate them with bun run --cwd packages/docs-site build-indexes whenever the API-doc model changed.

20206.content: The corpus pin and a consumer's declared dependency are different things, and conflating them is the first mistake a repo-wide find-and-replace makes. Several CLI tests hardcode archive URLs and extracted-entry paths, and some of them pin exactly the corpus string. packages/cli/src/library-match.test.ts, packages/cli/src/resolve.test.ts and packages/cli/src/druid-resolve-e2e.test.ts all carry a druid version literal in consumer archive URLs, and it can equal the ref the registry entry holds. That collision is the reason a repo-wide find-and-replace is unsafe: one copy of the version must move with the bump (the registry entry, and the provenance assertions named above), and another must not. normalizeSourceId (packages/cli/src/library-match.ts) strips /archive/<ref>.zip and matches on the repo name alone, so a consumer fixture is version-independent either way — which cuts both ways. Rewriting its version leaves the suite green, so a green bun test is not evidence the rewrite was correct. The 1.2.3 fixtures in packages/cli/src/library-scene-materialize.test.ts and the later resolve.test.ts cases are consumer fixtures on the same footing and equally out of scope. Leave them alone. A corpus bump changes the data folder, the floors, the emitted artifacts and the docs indexes. It does not change what a test project declares in its game.project.

20207.content: Then re-run bun run upstream:library-check — the repo you bumped should now report as current, and the issue the workflow opened can be closed.

20208.content: A curated target is only needed while its upstream ships no types resolve can use. Once an upstream release ships a types/ folder that resolve accepts, every project on that release gets those files in place of the curated copy, and the curated copy only costs a pin, a parity floor and a re-pin per release. bun run upstream:shipped-types-check reads the newest release of every repo behind a curated target, across the authored, LuaLS, script_api and native lanes, and runs its types/ folder through the same selection and compile check resolve applies: The newest release is the newest tag by commit date, or the default branch head for a repo with no tags. Each repo reports accepted, rejected with the check's first error, or none. A repo it could not read reports unknown and exits the command non-zero. The Library upstream check workflow runs the same sweep weekly and opens one issue per accepted repo, titled retire curated types for <slug>: <ref> ships types. The issue lists the shipped files and every curated entry the repo backs. The issue retires nothing. Retirement is a reviewed change, as pixels was (toolchain commit a32a1972), that removes each listed entry's registry entry, the input the issue lists for it, its /api page, vendored upstream source and parity floor, along with the tests that named it. Before making it, weigh the projects left behind: a project still on a release before the one that ships types has no types/ folder to fall back on once the curated copy is gone. An upstream maintainer gets the curated files to commit with export-types, as Shipping types with a library describes.

orderedDocs: 1. Add a fork to the library's library.json
2. Vendor the .d.ts and generate the artifacts
4. Surface parity against the upstream Lua
5. Cut the library over and validate
8bitskull / dicebag dicebag Dicebag is a Defold extension containing probability functions designed specifically for games.

A .tpatlas resource type for atlases exported from the TexturePacker tool, with an editor integration, a Bob build plugin, and a Defold exporter for TexturePacker. A .tpatlas works like a regular .atlas, including animations, but its images come from the exported .tpinfo file. Install the exporter in TexturePacker. Export a .tpinfo file. Create a Texture Packer Atlas in the editor and point it at that file. The skins example declares resource atlas properties and swaps a sprite image at runtime with go.set.

A base metallic-roughness PBR material with vertex and fragment shaders under /defold-pbr. The shaders read glTF material data populated by the model component and light data from Defold's built-in light components. Assign /defold-pbr/pbr.material to any model that should use the shader. Include pbr_lighting.glsl from an extension shader to add its own lighting terms. Models draw through a render script that sets the camera view and projection with render and camera. The material applies to model components.

A browser-based Defold code editor with live preview and console, usable as a stand-alone page or embedded in another web page. It includes an HTML5 template, static web resources, attachable go.script and gui.gui_script files, and the codepad.codepad Lua module. Set codepad/template.html as the HTML5 template. Add /codepad/bundle_resources/ to Bundle Resources. Require codepad.codepad from a script. Forward codepad.init(self, scenes), codepad.update(self, dt) and codepad.on_message(...) from the script's lifecycle functions. It runs only in a browser and talks to the page through html5. Each editable scene is loaded through a collectionproxy.

A build-time Bob plugin that encrypts resources in the game archive and a native runtime counterpart that registers a decryption function with the resource system. It uses the same XTEA algorithm as the engine but lets a project replace the default key or the algorithm itself. Fork the repository, add your fork's archive URL to game.project under [project] dependencies, then Fetch Libraries in the Defold editor. Change the key in both the Java plugin and src/plugin.cpp. Rebuild the plugin jar with build_plugin.sh after changing the build-time part. Expect no functions for scripts to call.
A collection of lowfi retro like sound effects.

A curated target is only needed while its upstream ships no types resolve can use. Once an upstream release ships a types/ folder that resolve accepts, every project on that release gets those files in place of the curated copy, and the curated copy only costs a pin, a parity floor and a re-pin per release. bun run upstream:shipped-types-check reads the newest release of every repo behind a curated target, across the authored, LuaLS, script_api and native lanes, and runs its types/ folder through the same selection and compile check resolve applies: The newest release is the newest tag by commit date, or the default branch head for a repo with no tags. Each repo reports accepted, rejected with the check's first error, or none. A repo it could not read reports unknown and exits the command non-zero. The Library upstream check workflow runs the same sweep weekly and opens one issue per accepted repo, titled retire curated types for <slug>: <ref> ships types. The issue lists the shipped files and every curated entry the repo backs. The issue retires nothing. Retirement is a reviewed change, as pixels was (toolchain commit a32a1972), that removes each listed entry's registry entry, the input the issue lists for it, its /api page, vendored upstream source and parity floor, along with the tests that named it. Before making it, weigh the projects left behind: a project still on a release before the one that ships types has no types/ folder to fall back on once the curated copy is gone. An upstream maintainer gets the curated files to commit with export-types, as Shipping types with a library describes.

A debug-only native extension that exposes a local HTTP bridge for inspecting and controlling a running game: scene and element queries, input with receipts, screenshots and optional desktop video recording. A bundled Python wrapper drives the bridge, and an opt-in automation_bridge Lua module lets scripts call publish, emit, command and annotate. Install the Python wrapper with the extension's install.py. Inspect scenes, send input and take screenshots; these need no Lua setup. Set application_api = 1 under [automation_bridge] in game.project to enable the Lua module.

A fork comment on a member upstream documents is an override of upstream's text, so it names the text it replaces. Its last line is @upstreamDoc and a 12-character pin, on a line of its own: The pin is a hash of upstream's whole LuaDoc block for that member, tags included, with whitespace collapsed, so re-indenting or re-wrapping upstream's comment keeps it and changing a word or a @param line does not. The pin never prints: the line is removed from the served declaration and the /api page. library check names every fork comment that prints upstream's doc instead, with the pin that would keep it: A notice never fails the check, so an update whose upstream edits a doc you override still lands; it prints upstream's new text until you read it, then either copy the pin into the fork's comment or delete the comment when upstream now says it well. A pin on a member upstream does not document guards nothing and is named as well. A pin shaped any other way, or placed anywhere but a module function's or constant's doc comment, stops the module from printing.

A library that requires a second library annotates the borrowed type by its bare name (druid's ---@field on_click event). Left alone that token resolves to nothing local and lowers to unknown. Naming its owner in externalTypes instead makes the emitter write a real import at the top of the declare module block and resolve every use of the token to it: emits import type { event } from 'event.event';, types all 46 of druid's callback fields as event, and resolves the ---@class event.on_size_changed: event parent to a real extends. The import is type-only, so it binds no value and a library that exports a function of the same name (quest.event) still compiles. The key is the LuaLS token as written; module must be the owning target's moduleId exactly, and name its exported type. A token whose local name would collide with one the library declares itself fails loudly rather than silently shadowing it. The consuming project must declare that upstream library too. resolve builds no inter-library dependency graph, so a project that lists druid alone gets druid.druid without event.event — the import then degrades to an error-any under the repo-wide skipLibCheck. Declare both; druid does not run without event.event at runtime either. quest and token import event from event.event the same way (quest also imports queue), so a project that lists either one declares defold-event beside it. Prefer externalTypes over a typeRenames entry pointing at an import(...) type: the api-doc lowering maps through the same context, so an inline import('event.event').event would render as the user-facing signature on the library's /api page, where externalTypes renders the clean event. A runtime require is not by itself a type dependency, so decide from the annotations rather than the requires. panthera opens panthera/panthera.lua with local tweener = require("tweener.tweener"), yet no annotation in its subtree names a tweener type — every easing is annotated string|constant. It therefore takes no externalTypes entry, and a project consuming panthera needs defold-tweener installed for it to run but not for its types to resolve — the inverse of druid, which needs event.event for both.

A Lua preprocessor that hooks into the Lua builder plugin system in bob, the Defold build tool. It strips or keeps code at build time based on --#IF, --#ELSE and --#ENDIF blocks that test the RELEASE, DEBUG or HEADLESS keywords. Use Defold 1.4.2 or higher. Wrap code in the conditional comment blocks. Write --DEBUG_ASSERT(...) to include an assert only in debug builds.

A measured target's printed declaration does not stop at the fork. Where upstream documents a module-level member and the fork does not override it with a pinned comment, upstream's own LuaDoc summary, parameter docs and return docs are printed as that member's doc comment, so a project's editor shows them on hover. The api-doc is lowered from the same printed declaration, so the /api page shows the same text, marked so a reader can tell it apart from the fork's own prose. Six rules bound it: Parameter and return docs follow the declared signature. The summary ends at the first line starting with @. Each @param or @tparam text prints as an @param on every declaration that lists that parameter, in the declaration's order, so an overload carries only its own; @return or @treturn text prints as @returns unless the declaration returns void, and a constant takes no tags. Types never print: a ---@param line is read as LuaLS (name type description), every other line as LDoc (name description, a (type) or a @tparam type dropped), and a following line that opens no tag continues the text. A tag with no description, a vararg ..., and a dotted table field such as config.dsn print nothing. An @ after a space, such as LDoc's @{name} reference, prints as \@ so TypeScript reads it as text rather than as a tag. One blank line inside a comment run does not end the block. Upstream often wraps a long @param list around a blank line, which would otherwise truncate the block to its tag half and lose the summary above it. The blank is crossed only when the segment touching the definition opens no --- block of its own, so a blank-separated section header above a documented member never merges into it, and only ever one blank is crossed. A brief never restates its own symbol. Where upstream writes the member's name as the block's first line and the summary beneath it, the name line is dropped, so the rendered brief is the summary rather than the symbol you are already reading. A first line that merely mentions the name is prose and survives; a block that is only the name imports nothing at all. Fork prose wins only while pinned. A member upstream documents keeps exactly what the fork wrote, on every overload, only while the fork's comment carries an @upstreamDoc pin matching upstream's current text (see Pinning a fork comment); a pinned comment replaces upstream's tags as well as its summary. Without a pin, or with a stale one, upstream's summary, parameter docs and return docs replace the fork's summary and its @param and @returns tags; every other tag, such as @noSelf or @deprecated, stays. A member upstream does not document keeps the fork's comment, pinned or not. A comment holding only tags, such as / @noSelf /, is not a summary: the print puts upstream's doc at the top of that same block, and an @param or @returns the fork wrote there keeps its slot. Only the module's own members. The merge fills the functions and constants directly inside the declare module block. A file-scope global and a member of a nested namespace keep whatever the fork wrote. The import is printed, never vendored. fork/<moduleId>.d.ts is untouched and the print changes comments only, so the identity diff on types still proves the emit is lossless, imported prose stays distinguishable from the fork's forever after, and an upstream doc change reaches the print with no hand edit. A block whose every segment opens with a plain -- rather than --- is refused, and counted as refusedDocBlocksTotal on the target's parity report. Nothing distinguishes such a block from a section header sitting above a run of constants — monarch's -- transition messages and boom's -- initialize boom are the same shape to any parser — so admitting the class would attach one member's heading to another's documentation. The remedy is to author that member's doc-comment in the fork, where a human makes the judgment and the result correctly renders as first-party. refusedDocBlocks charges only the refusals still unanswered, so the remedy actually clears it: write the brief and the member stops counting. A member the fork deliberately does not declare is excused by its parityException instead — there is no element to hang a brief on, and the ledger already carries a human's reading of that same comment, which is why boom's five lifecycle blocks charge nothing. A merely missingMembers name is not excused: its remedy is declaring it. The raw term is what keeps the refusal itself visible — defmath writes all 36 of its blocks that way and charges none of them, every one being answered in the fork's own words. An imported symbol's /api heading carries a U dot labelled Documentation imported from upstream, beside the G dot an ambient global carries. The page's provenance block already names the repo and ref the text came from.

A native extension for HTML5 builds that integrates the Facebook Instant Games API. It registers an fbinstant Lua module with functions such as fbinstant.initialize, fbinstant.start_game, fbinstant.get_player and fbinstant.show_rewarded_video. Configure the HTML5 section of game.project. Start from the engine HTML template and the example collections covering ads, context, leaderboards, payments and player data.

A native extension for KaiOS web builds. It provides a modified engine HTML template, maps the left softkey, right softkey and call keys to KEY_F1, KEY_F2 and KEY_MENU, and registers a kaios Lua module with kaios.exit, kaios.play_sound and kaios.stop_sound. Include the sound files with the bundle resources setting in game.project, since kaios.play_sound plays them through the JavaScript AudioContext. For KaiAds integration, use the separate extension-kaiads repository upstream points to.

A native extension that adds a .simpledata component type, editable in the editor and built by a Bob plugin. Each component holds preset fields such as name, f32, i32, v3 and an array_f32 list. It also serves as an example of adding a custom resource and component type. Add .simpledata components to game objects. Read single fields with go.get. Read the whole float array into a Lua table with simpledata.get_array_f32(url). Component fields are read through go (go.get), including indexed access to array_f32.

A native extension that adds a Vulkan graphics adapter, used when the device supports Vulkan and falling back to OpenGL otherwise. It links MoltenVK on macOS and iOS. It adds no functions for scripts to call. Enable shader.output_spirv, or builds fail to compile. To build with Vulkan only, exclude the OpenGL adapter through an application manifest.

A native extension that implements the Poco test automation API, so Python test scripts on a computer can dump the scene graph and send clicks, swipes and key events to a running game. It ships the poco.lua.defold-poco Lua server module and a native poco_helper module (dump, click, swipe, keyevent), plus a test project and Python example scripts. require('poco.lua.defold-poco') in a script or GUI script. Call poco:init_server(15004) in init. Call poco:server_loop() in update. Add custom functions the client can call with poco:set_dispatch_fn. poco:set_view_proj and poco:set_gui_view_proj take view projection matrices built with vmath, which default to the identity matrix.

A native extension that runs a Defold game server against the Amazon GameLift Server SDK, with prebuilt SDK libraries for Linux and macOS. It registers a gamelift Lua module with functions such as gamelift.init, gamelift.process_ready and gamelift.accept_player_session. The repository also contains an example client project. On the server, call gamelift.init with a port and listener functions for session start, process termination and health checks. Report readiness with gamelift.process_ready.

A native extension wrapping the Epic Online Services SDK, bundling SDK libraries for Windows, Linux and macOS. It registers an eos Lua module with functions such as eos.init, eos.get_achievement_definitions and eos.get_stats_definitions. Do not rely on it yet: the upstream README marks the extension as work in progress and not ready for use, and gives no installation steps. See the example main.script, which calls eos.init with product, sandbox, deployment and client credentials before querying achievement and stats definitions.

A native or hybrid library that ships an extension .script_api (the same YAML format every Defold extension ships) has a third ingestion mode, distinct from the LuaLS front-end above: packages/cli/src/library/sync-script-api-types.ts, driven by the scriptApi list of a library's recipe.json. Instead of parsing ---@ annotations, it routes the committed .script_api snapshot through the shared ref-doc emitter — scriptApiToFixtureJson → generateModuleDeclaration, the exact path resolve-time extension typing uses — so one-level nested sub-namespaces (bridge.platform, bridge.achievements) survive into nested namespace blocks. The output is an importable module keyed by moduleId (declare module 'bridge.bridge'), matching the LuaLS library goldens, so the library imports under its pinned specifier; the declare global form stays the resolve emitter's, for extensions a project declares. Each entry names scriptApi (the path to the .script_api in the repo), moduleId, namespace, and the exact apiDoc / fidelity output paths; the library folder pins repo and ref as above. The generate arms mirror the LuaLS ones: The first migrated target is Playgama/bridge-defold (pinned v2.3.0), maintained entirely from its .script_api — its former ts-defold binding is gone. Three things are specific to a script_api target and worth knowing: Output paths are pinned explicitly and named for the single-segment namespace. Like the LuaLS libraries, a migrated script_api library is the sole maintainer of its namespace, so its goldens are api-doc/bridge.json and fidelity/bridge.json — not the dotted moduleId — which keeps the docs Libraries tree and the file layout uniform with druid. The require specifier is still the moduleId (declare module 'bridge.bridge'), so resolve prints it under that specifier. Fidelity mirrors the emitter, so an unmapped token counts against coverage. The report is computed over the ref-doc doc with the emitter's own type map: a token the emitter renders as unknown is counted in unknownFallbacks and listed in unknownTokens rather than hidden. A pipe-separated type: or a YAML list (type: [table, string]) is split into one token per alternative before that check, so bridge's string | nil returns resolve to string | undefined and bridge lands at coverage 1. A slot left with no token at all counts as one unknown fallback, listed as (untyped), so it cannot pass as covered. A parameter upstream calls omittable in prose only is declared, not inferred. The .script_api format cannot say that a middle parameter may be left out with the later ones shifting left, and upstream sometimes describes a trailing parameter as optional without marking it optional: true. A target lists either kind of slot under omittableSlots (element, slot, and the upstream evidence that allows it), and the emitted declaration carries two overloads, with and without it. The api-doc page and the fidelity report stay as upstream wrote them. A slot the fixture no longer has fails the emit, so the entry cannot go stale.

A placeholder for an Android in-app update extension built on the Play Core in-app updates feature. At this revision the native code is still the extension template: it registers a myextension Lua module whose only function, myextension.reverse, reverses a string. Expect no in-app update calls yet: the upstream README describes the Play Core feature but gives no installation steps. See the example script, which calls myextension.reverse and prints the result.

A placeholder repository for a Defold extension to integrate the Google Play Integrity API. At this revision it contains only a README and a license, with no extension code, Lua module, or example project. Expect nothing to use yet: no callable API is provided at this revision.

A repository described as a WebTransport implementation for Defold. At this revision it contains only a README and a license, with no extension code, content or Lua API. Expect nothing to use yet: this revision adds nothing to a project.

A small native extension that encodes and decodes QR codes, using quirc for decoding. It registers a qrcode Lua module with qrcode.scan, which reads the text from an image buffer, and qrcode.generate, which returns a QR code image buffer and its side length. See the included example app, which scans camera images and creates QR codes; it depends on a camera extension that supports only macOS, iOS and Android. Both functions work on buffer objects: scan expects a first stream of UINT8 3 texels, and generate returns a data stream of UINT8 1.

A work-in-progress native extension for the OneTrust SDK that upstream describes as not working. On Android it registers an onetrust Lua module whose only function, onetrust.init, is currently an empty stub; other platforms get a null extension with no module. Guard the call with if onetrust then onetrust.init() end, as the example script does, since the module exists only on Android.

A work-in-progress PBR core with shaders, a material, a reference render script and the defold-pbr/core Lua module. Editor scripts generate environment lighting assets from .hdr files and extract .glb content into Defold collections. Attach /defold-pbr/core.script to a game object to create the PBR context. Require defold-pbr/core to call functions such as set_environment, add_light_point and set_camera_world. In the render script, pass get_constants() to the model draw call and wrap it in enable_textures() and disable_textures(). The module builds its constant buffer and binds textures with render, and reads texture handles with resource.

After library check --api-doc-out, open api-doc/<namespace>.json and inspect info.description. It carries the description line on the library's main ---@class. When that class has no description line the value is empty (""), and the /api page renders with no description — the "every library page has a non-empty description" gate fails. Remediate by adding a namespace-keyed entry to <data folder>/library-descriptions.json — "<namespace>": "<one-line summary>", keyed by namespace. The site's fallback in api-surface-loader.ts reads it for LuaLS libraries (a ts-defold library keys its fallback on the upstream classification dir; a LuaLS library has none, so it keys on the namespace directly). druid needs nothing here — its ---@class druid is described, so it never reaches the fallback. decore is the worked example: its ---@class carries no description, its api-doc/decore.json info.description is "", and the committed "decore": "Defold ECS Data Manager" entry supplies the page description.

An advanced example native extension that retrieves profiling data at runtime, with the counters available even in release builds. It registers a profile Lua module whose profile.get_properties returns a table of the latest counters. Call profile.get_properties() each update and print the result, as the example project's main.script does. Expect the regular profiler normally included in Defold to be removed, as upstream notes.

An authored .d.ts has no upstream source to regenerate from, so every future upstream API change is a manual edit to the vendored declaration. That is the standing cost. Weigh it against the gain of severing ts-defold: a first-party authored surface is authored-here, carries its own upstream repo/tag pin (not the shared ts-defold/library commit), and is maintained on the toolchain repo's own cadence rather than inherited from a third-party vendoring. Fork — copy the retired ts-defold .d.ts verbatim as the first-party fixture. Zero fidelity risk (the surface is identical to what shipped), and the provenance moves to the real upstream. Best when the ts-defold binding is already correct and the surface is small and stable, so the manual-maintenance cost is low. Hand-author — write a fresh .d.ts from the library's documentation. Only worth it when the ts-defold binding is wrong or absent and the surface is small enough to author confidently. Keep — leave the library ts-defold-sourced. Correct when the surface is large or churns often, so the manual-maintenance cost outweighs the provenance gain, or when a generated lane is likely to become available. Spent for the current corpus: every library the ts-defold registry once carried has severed and library-targets.json holds "targets": [] (see 5. Cut the library over and validate), so a library reaching this decision today has no ts-defold binding to keep — the real choice is fork versus hand-author.

An energysaver.go game object with a script and a GUI dimmer that lower power use after a period of input inactivity. It reduces the frame rate, dims the screen by 50%, and finally disables rendering, each on its own configurable delay. Drag energysaver.go into the bootstrap collection. Tune its script properties. Set the is_energy_saving_allowed property with go.set to pause the savings temporarily, for example during cutscenes. The script drives sys (sys.set_update_frequency, sys.set_render_enabled), timer for the inactivity delays, and gui for the dimming overlay.

An example native extension for Android that combines C++, .java sources, a .jar, a prebuilt static library and Android resources. On Android it registers the androidnative Lua module with functions such as vibrate, getraw and multiply; other platforms get a stub extension with no module. Build the project for Android. Check that androidnative is not nil before calling it, as the example menu GUI script does. See the java_src and lib_src build scripts for how the .jar and .a files are produced.

An example native extension for the HTML5 platform showing plain C++ code, a prebuilt Emscripten library, inline JavaScript through EM_ASM, and an Emscripten JavaScript library. It registers an html5nativeext Lua module with demonstration functions such as html5nativeext.multiply, html5nativeext.fibonacci and html5nativeext.get_user_data. Build the project for HTML5; the repository is an example project rather than a packaged library. Call the module's functions as its main.script does, including polling html5nativeext.get_user_data for data set from the web page.

An example native extension that decodes .webm video into a buffer, with no sound support. Upstream marks it as an example not meant for production use. It registers a videoplayer Lua module with functions such as videoplayer.open, videoplayer.get_frame and videoplayer.update. Load the video with resource.load. Open it with videoplayer.open. Call videoplayer.update each frame and upload the frame buffer to a texture. The example loads the video and writes each frame with resource (resource.load, resource.set_texture); the frame is a buffer with one RGB stream, shown on a sprite.

An HTML5 native extension that integrates the Web Monetization JavaScript API, so a game can detect whether a player has an active payment stream. It registers a webmonetization Lua module with is_monetized, set_listener and EVENT constants for the stream state. Set payment_pointer in a [webmonetization] section of game.project. Call webmonetization.is_monetized() or register a listener with webmonetization.set_listener to react to payment events.

append(task: ((value: unknown) => unknown) | promise): promise Append a task to this promise's internal sequence without reassigning. The task may return a value or a promise. If task is a promise, the pipeline waits for it to finish and adopts its result. The incoming value is not forwarded into task (same as append(function() return task end)). Returns self for chaining. astar.setup(map_width: number, map_height: number, direction: number, allocate: number, typical_adjacent: number, cache[optional]: boolean, use_zero[optional]: boolean, map_vflip[optional]: boolean, map_id[optional]: number) Initial setup. You have to setup the astar before calling any other methods. map_width — Width of your map. This is generally width of your tilemap. map_height — Height of your map. This is generally width of your tilemap. direction — Movement direction (astar.DIRECTION_FOUR or astar.DIRECTION_EIGHT) astar.DIRECTION_FOUR - on a square grid that allows 4 directions of movement using Manhattan distance. astar.DIRECTION_EIGHT - on a square grid that allows 8 directions of movement using Euclidean distance. allocate — How many states should be internally allocated at a time. This can be hard to get correct. The higher the value, the more memory Patfinder will use. If you have a small map (a few thousand states?) it may make sense to pass in the maximum value. This will cache everything, and MicroPather will only need one main memory allocation. For a chess board, allocate would be set to 8x8 (64) If your map is large, something like 1/4 the number of possible states is good. If your state space is huge, use a multiple (5-10x) of the normal path. "Occasionally" call astar.reset_cache() to free unused memory. typical_adjacent — Used to determine cache size. The typical number of adjacent states to a given state. (On a chessboard, 8.) Higher values use a little more memory. cache[optional] — Turn on path caching. Uses more memory (yet again) but at a huge speed advantage if you may call the pather with the same path or sub-path, which is common for pathing over maps in games. Default is true use_zero[optional] — Toggle start index 0 or 1 for tables and tile positions. Also you can set it by call astar.use_zero(). Default is false map_vflip[optional] — Flips the map vertically. This doesn't flip the coordinates. Also you can set it by call astar.map_vflip(). Default is false map_id[optional] — ID of the map. Has to be an integer from 0 to 2^16 - 1. Default is 0.
