britzl/defcon is a plain-Lua console library with no .script_api and no ---@ annotations, so it is a Bucket-E authored target. Its ts-defold binding was a correct 24-line single-module surface, and the surface is small and stable — exactly the low-maintenance-cost case the fork path is for. Keeping it ts-defold-sourced would forgo the provenance gain for no real saving; a fresh hand-author would be redundant work when the existing binding is already right. So the decision is fork: copy the retired .d.ts verbatim, sever ts-defold, and pin to the real upstream. The reference defcon/library.json: and defcon/reviewed.json pins { "ref": "2.6.0" }. authored vendors the fork; moduleId defcon.console names the declare module a consumer imports; namespace defcon is the single-segment artifact stem, so the golden is api-doc/defcon.json — not the dotted moduleId — keeping the docs Libraries tree and file layout uniform with the other bare-stem severed libraries. Nothing else owned defcon, so it was free to take; orthographic.camera below is the case where it is not. The defcon page then attributes to britzl/defcon at 2.6.0, not the ts-defold/library corpus.

britzl/defold-orthographic (a camera suite, pinned to tag 3.6.3) is a second markdown no-go that answered fork, and it settles two questions persist's surface never raised. Which namespace does the fork publish under? persist took the bare persist. orthographic cannot: it is the markdown lane's one registered target, so api-doc/orthographic.json is already a committed regeneration proof owned by that lane, and the no-go hides the bare orthographic namespace from page enumeration. Forking under it would overwrite the proofs and render no page. So the authored target keeps the dotted orthographic.camera — the nakama.engine.defold shape — which takes over the retired ts-defold module name and leaves the route and import string byte-identical. The rule generalizes: when the retired module name already equals the publish namespace, fork onto it; only reach for a bare namespace when nothing else owns it. Which file do you copy? The ts-defold lane runs a type-mapping pass, so fixtures/ts-defold/orthographic.camera.d.ts says hash/url/vmath.vector3 while the codemodded output says Hash/Url/Vector3. persist's two forms were identical, so the template never had to choose. Copy the codemodded output — the authored lane emits its input verbatim, so forking the raw fixture would ship ts-defold's upstream type names and fail the declaration-validity gate. Forking the codemodded output makes the cutover a byte-for-byte no-op, which is what lets you prove the severance and any type correction as two separate diffs. orthographic then took that second diff: upstream documents follow as accepting one game object or a table of them, and the ts-defold binding typed only the singular target: Hash | Url. On a file the toolchain repo now owns, widening it to targets: Hash | Url | (Hash | Url)[] is a one-line edit plus a re-emit. It moves no recorded gate number — the fidelity comparison scores member names, the unknown token, parameter count, return void-ness, and optionality, and a rename plus a union widening touches none of them. The third diff is the signature correction, and unlike the second it does move name sets. The fork gained get_automatic_zoom and set_automatic_zoom (live API upstream defines and ts-defold never had), lost add_projector, get_projection_id and use_projector (deprecated stubs whose upstream body only error()s), and world_to_screen narrowed to the (camera_id, world) upstream actually reads — its third adjust_mode argument was silently ignored at runtime, so narrowing it is breaking on purpose. With nine ledger entries covering the withdrawn stubs and the three camera.script lifecycle hooks, the target reaches callableCoverage: 1. The markdown verdict is re-derived over the new export list and lands on the same no-go. The fourth diff is the field correction, which moves the constants half of that same list: MSG_SET_AUTOMATIC_ZOOM was declared from the pinned camera.lua, and MSG_USE_PROJECTION and ORTHOGRAPHIC_RENDER_SCRIPT_USED were deleted, upstream defining neither anywhere — reading either returned nil, so the deletion is breaking on paper only. The verdict is re-derived a second time and holds: the nineteen constants and five functions the README's API table does not cover are still the surface loss that drove it.

britzl/deftest (a test runner, pinned to 2.8.0) is a second fork with the same reference-entry shape as defcon.console. It illustrates one wrinkle: its .d.ts declares ambient top-level globals (describe, before, after, test, assert) alongside declare module 'deftest.deftest'. A fork copies the surface verbatim, so those globals carry into the printed declaration and therefore into the dts-declaration-validity gate's compilation. That is fine — they raise no duplicate-identifier clash — and the api-doc lowering publishes them alongside the module's exports (add, run), each marked as an ambient global so the reference page distinguishes what the import reaches from what is callable without it. Do not alter a vendored fork to suppress such globals; they are part of the library's real surface. A file-scope type is held to a stricter rule than a file-scope value: it publishes only when a published signature names it and it carries members (an interface, or a type alias over an object literal). A union, a function type, or an internal generic helper stays off the page, so a fork's incidental type machinery does not become reference content.

Build-time Lua obfuscation using Prometheus, hooked into the Lua builder plugin system in bob, the Defold build tool. Scripts are obfuscated as they are built; the extension adds no Lua module for game scripts to call. Fork the repository, as upstream asks, add your fork's archive URL to game.project under [project] dependencies, then Fetch Libraries in the Defold editor. Put a Prometheus configuration file named prometheus.lua in the project root. Set disabled = 1 under a [prometheus] section in game.project to turn obfuscation off.

Build-time support for Teal, a typed dialect of Lua. A Bob plugin compiles and type checks .tl files during the build, and an editor script registers a Teal language server. The native part is an empty extension. Use Defold 1.8.1 or later. Create a tlconfig.lua in the project root. Require .tl files from scripts and Lua modules as if they were .lua files.

compute(node: Flow_Element, x: number, y: number, w: number, h: number) Compute layout for a node tree. Writes layout.x/y/w/h to every node in the tree recursively, using bottom-left origin coordinates. Algorithm: 1. Measure all regular (non-overlay) children to sum fixed sizes and flex_grow weights. 2. Distribute remaining free space according to justify_content. 3. Place each child along the main axis, applying align_items / align_self on the cross axis. 4. Recurse into each child. 5. Layout overlay children (popup, bottom_sheet) at full parent bounds as a final pass. node — The root element to compute layout for x — Left edge of the available area in layout space (px) y — Bottom edge of the available area in layout space (px) w — Available width in pixels h — Available height in pixels

Both buffers must carry a uint8 rgb stream of three or four components per pixel and hold at least width height elements. decode_rgb(png: string, premultiply_alpha?: boolean): LuaMultiReturn<[ Opaque<"buffer"> & { length: LuaLengthMethod<number>; }, number, number ] | [ undefined, undefined, undefined ]> Decodes a valid PNG into an RGB buffer with one uint8 pixels stream of three components per pixel. The decoded rows are flipped vertically to match Defold's buffer orientation. The extension ignores LodePNG's decode error, so a corrupt PNG may crash the engine instead of returning nils. Three nils mean the buffer could not be created or failed validation, so check the buffer before reading the dimensions. png — The PNG bytes, which must be a valid PNG. premultiply_alpha — Accepted for symmetry with {@link png.decode_rgba}; it only has effect in the RGBA path. The pixel buffer, its width and its height, or three nils when the buffer cannot be created or fails validation.

decode_rgba(png: string, premultiply_alpha?: boolean): LuaMultiReturn<[ Opaque<"buffer"> & { length: LuaLengthMethod<number>; }, number, number ] | [ undefined, undefined, undefined ]> Decodes a valid PNG into an RGBA buffer with one uint8 pixels stream of four components per pixel. The decoded rows are flipped vertically to match Defold's buffer orientation. The extension ignores LodePNG's decode error, so a corrupt PNG may crash the engine instead of returning nils. Three nils mean the buffer could not be created or failed validation, so check the buffer before reading the dimensions. png — The PNG bytes, which must be a valid PNG. premultiply_alpha — Multiply each pixel's color components by its alpha while decoding. The pixel buffer, its width and its height, or three nils when the buffer cannot be created or fails validation.

dev-masih / defarmy defarmy Groups game objects (soldiers) into armies, places them in a built-in or customized pattern, and moves and rotates each army as a group. Create an army with army_create and a soldier for each game object with soldier_create, then call soldier_move from each soldier's update and apply the position and rotation it returns.

dev-masih / defgraph defgraph Builds a world map as a graph of nodes and routes that can change at any time, draws it for debugging, and moves game objects along it with a built-in pathfinder. Add nodes with map_add_node and join them with map_add_route, start each game object with move_initialize, then call move_player from its update and apply the position and rotation it returns. Every library whose types the toolchain ships is pinned to one upstream ref in one of five lane registries: the LuaLS, script_api and authored registries, with the fixtures their entries name, sit in the newest data folder, packages/library-types/data/<version>/, and the markdown and OpenAPI registries at the root of packages/library-types/ in a toolchain checkout. Upstream keeps moving; the pins do not. This page is what to do when one of them has fallen behind. Authoring LuaLS library types and Authoring forked library types cover adding a library. This page covers moving one that is already there, which is a different job: the generation commands are the easy half, and the couplings that move with the pin are the half that is not discoverable from the sync scripts. This page is for maintainers of the library data in the toolchain repo, changed by pull requests there. Consuming a library in your own project is resolve, and your project's declared dependency version is unrelated to the pin here. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root unless a step names another folder.

facebook.login_with_permissions(permissions: table, audience: number, callback: function) Login to Facebook and request a set of publish permissions. The user is prompted to authorize the application using the login dialog of the specific platform. Even if the user is already logged in to Facebook this function can still be used to request additional publish permissions. A comprehensive list of permissions can be found in the Facebook permissions documentation, as well as in their guide to best practices for login management. Log in to Facebook with a set of publish permissions Log in to Facebook with a set of read permissions permissions — table with the requested publish permission strings. audience — The audience that should be able to see the publications. Can be any of facebook.AUDIENCE_NONE facebook.AUDIENCE_ONLYME facebook.AUDIENCE_FRIENDS facebook.AUDIENCE_EVERYONE callback — Callback function that is executed when the permission request dialog is closed.

facebook.login_with_tracking_preference(login_tracking: number, permissions: table, crypto_nonce: string, callback: function) iOS ONLY. Login to Facebook and request a set of permissions. Allows developers to signal that a login is limited in terms of tracking users. The user is prompted to authorize the application using the login dialog of the specific platform. Even if the user is already logged in to Facebook this function can still be used to request additional publish permissions. A comprehensive list of permissions can be found in the Facebook permissions documentation, as well as in their guide to best practices for login management. For Limited Login the list of permissions can be found in the Permissions in Limited Login documentation. Log in to Facebook with a set of publish permissions Log in to Facebook with a set of read permissions login_tracking — The tracking type for the login. Can be any of facebook.LOGIN_TRACKING_LIMITED facebook.LOGIN_TRACKING_ENABLED permissions — table with the requested publish permission strings. crypto_nonce — Nonce that the configuration was created with. A unique nonce will be used if none is provided to the factory method. callback — Callback function that is executed when the permission request dialog is closed.

facebook.show_dialog(dialog: string, param: table, callback: function) Show facebook web dialog Display a Facebook web dialog of the type specified in the dialog parameter. The param table should be set up according to the requirements of each dialog type. Note that some parameters are mandatory. Below is the list of available dialogs and where to find Facebook's developer documentation on parameters and response data. "apprequests" Shows a Game Request dialog. Game Requests allows players to invite their friends to play a game. Available parameters [type:string] title [type:string] message [type:number] action_type [type:number] filters [type:string] data [type:string] object_id [type:table] suggestions [type:table] recipients [type:string] to On success, the "result" table parameter passed to the callback function will include the following fields [type:string] request_id [type:table] to Details for each parameter "feed" The Feed Dialog allows people to publish individual stories to their timeline. [type:string] caption [type:string] description [type:string] picture [type:string] link [type:table] people_ids [type:string] place_id [type:string] ref On success, the "result" table parameter passed to the callback function will include the following fields [type:string] post_id Details for each parameter "appinvite" The App Invite dialog is available only on iOS and Android. Note that the url parameter corresponds to the appLinkURL (iOS) and setAppLinkUrl (Android) properties. fidelity/<namespace>.json tells you whether the emit is worth committing: coverage — the fraction of type tokens that resolved to a known type. Druid sits around 0.9; a healthy new library lands in the same range. Near-zero means the source is not meaningfully annotated — reconsider the target. unknownTokens — the distinct type names that fell back to unknown. A cross- library reference (another Insality module) shows up here until you name its owner in externalTypes, which resolves it; the LuaLS placeholders and a bare ... are not among them, because they declare no type and now lower to unknown without counting against coverage, and neither is a bare function, because it now lowers to the callable type (...args: any[]) => unknown. A rename that should have applied shows up as an unexpected entry — fix typeRenames and re-emit. undocumentedMembers — members with no annotation at all; informational. Each report's coverage is pinned by a committed floor, the module's entry in floors in the library's library.json, so a regeneration that lowers it fails the suite instead of quietly rewriting the report, and library check measures the module against the same floor. Regenerating never touches the floors; when you genuinely improve coverage, lock the win in with which raises each floor to the current coverage and can never lower one. A drop is therefore always a real regression to fix at the source, never a floor to edit down.

Four lanes fetch and regenerate. Run their commands from the toolchain root, in order, after editing the pinned ref: | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ----- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | LuaLS | the library folder's reviewed.json | bun run --cwd packages/library-types luals:fetch, then luals:fidelity, api-doc | | Lane | Pin | Commands | | -------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Markdown | markdown-targets.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-markdown-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --api-doc | | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | OpenAPI | openapi-targets.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-openapi-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --api-doc | | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ---------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | script_api | the library folder's reviewed.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-script-api-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --data packages/library-types/data, then bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc | A library folder sits in the newest version-named folder of packages/library-types/data/, named for its repository: its <host>/<owner>/<repo>, lowercased, without .git. --fetch is the only step that touches the network; everything after it reads the committed fixtures, so a regeneration is reproducible offline. No lane writes a declaration: resolve prints each target's types from its fixtures, so check them by printing them with bun test packages/cli/src/library from the toolchain root. Set GITHUB_TOKEN before fetching. The fetchers read it (sync-luals-types.ts and sync-library-types.ts both send it as a bearer token) and GitHub degrades unauthenticated API traffic — the git/trees calls behind --fetch and upstream:library-check can return 504 Gateway Timeout on every attempt while the rate-limit budget still shows requests remaining, so a 504 here is not evidence that the pin or the repo is wrong. The authored lane is the exception, and it is the one that surprises people. A library's forks have no --fetch and no fidelity pass. Their source/upstream/ snapshots are vendored by hand and their .d.ts is hand-written, so bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc is the only command they take. Refreshing an authored pin means: edit the ref in the library folder's reviewed.json; copy the upstream files named by upstreamLua into the library folder's source/upstream/… by hand (the path under it mirrors the upstream path); update the hand-written .d.ts for whatever the new upstream added or changed; re-run bun run --cwd packages/library-types parity and bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc.

get_modules_download_progress(module_names: string | string[]): liveupdater_download_progress Byte-based progress for a module or a set of modules, with a per-resolution breakdown in the low/high fields. Shared dependency archives are counted once per set; an archive identical in both manifests counts toward the resolution counted first (for RES_BOTH that is lowres — the pass that actually downloads it). Anchored to the download queue: an archive counts as downloaded when nothing for it is pending, so the result reaches 100 exactly when the set's downloads drain. For by_request modules that were not requested yet, the future queue content is predicted from the same rules enqueue_modules uses; that prediction can dip for a moment while a shared archive is remounted to its highres copy, it recovers on the next mount.

gpgs.achievement_get() Get information about all achievement's state asynchronously. Result return to callback previously set by gpgs.set_callback with message_id == gpgs.MSG_GET_ACHIEVEMENTS. Result is an array of JSON strings. Decode each string with json.decode() to get a table containing the following fields id - achievement id (from GP console) name - achievement name description - achievement description xp - how much experience points will be added when achievement will be unlocked steps - current step of incremental achievement total_steps - total amount of steps of incremental achievement unlocked - set to true if achievement is unlocked. Otherwise field is missed. hidden - set to true if achievement is hidden. Otherwise field is missed. revealed - set to true if achievement is revealed. Otherwise field is missed.

gpgs.event_get() Get information about all events asynchronously. Result returns to callback previously set by gpgs.set_callback with message_id == gpgs.MSG_GET_EVENTS. Result is an array of JSON strings. Decode each string with json.decode() to get a table containing the following fields id - event id formatted_value - sum of all increments have been made to this event value - the number of increments this user has made to this event description - event's description image - URI that can be used to load the event's image icon name - event's name visible - whether the event should be displayed to the user in any event related UIs

levelplay.create_banner_ad(ad_unit_id: string, options?: table): number Creates a reusable banner ad view after successful initialization. Its ad-unit ID and all options are fixed for the view's lifetime. Create it once, then load, hide, show, and auto-refresh the same handle until it is permanently destroyed. ad_unit_id — Banner ad-unit ID from the LevelPlay dashboard. options — Creation-time banner configuration. These fields apply to every load and show; changing one requires destroying the handle and creating a new banner. handle — Positive handle, or nil when native creation is rejected.

levelplay.create_interstitial_ad(ad_unit_id: string, bid_floor?: number): number Creates a reusable interstitial ad object after successful initialization. Its ad-unit ID and optional bid floor are fixed for the object's lifetime. Create it once, then use the returned handle for multiple load/show cycles with the same ad-unit ID and creation configuration. ad_unit_id — Interstitial ad-unit ID from the LevelPlay dashboard. bid_floor — Optional minimum eCPM in USD. It applies to every load by this object; changing it requires destroying the handle and creating a new object. handle — Positive handle, or nil when native creation is rejected.

levelplay.create_rewarded_ad(ad_unit_id: string, bid_floor?: number): number Creates a reusable rewarded ad object after successful initialization. Its ad-unit ID and optional bid floor are fixed for the object's lifetime. Create it once, then use the returned handle for multiple load/show cycles with the same ad-unit ID and creation configuration. ad_unit_id — Rewarded ad-unit ID from the LevelPlay dashboard. bid_floor — Optional minimum eCPM in USD. It applies to every load by this object; changing it requires destroying the handle and creating a new object. handle — Positive handle, or nil when native creation is rejected.

Neither number is "the" coverage of a target, and no single figure replaces them. A module can agree completely on one axis while missing the other entirely, so folding them into one mean would let each mask the other — exactly the reading the split exists to prevent. platypus is the worked case. It defines one module function and 14 constants, so its callableCoverage is 1 over a single comparison while its fieldCoverage is 1 over fourteen. Both read the same, and they are not the same result: one is a single create agreeing on arity, the other is fourteen constants each found by name. Averaged into one figure the module would look uniformly verified, and the single number would move by a fourteenth for a defect on either side — which is why the two are reported separately whether they agree or not. Read the two together. A perfect callableCoverage over a handful of functions still says nothing about a large upstreamFields, and a perfect fieldCoverage says nothing about arity. A phantom on either axis enters no coverage figure, having no upstream member to be a fraction of, so it is visible only in its list.

None of these are visible from the sync scripts, and each of them reds ci if you skip it. The committed floor. floors in the library's library.json holds a per-module measurement the gates and library check assert against. New upstream surface changes the measurement, so the floor entry moves with the pin — raise a generated module's ratio with bun run --cwd packages/library-types fidelity:floor, and edit a fork's or native extension's { callable, field } pair by hand. The parity reports. authored-parity-floor.test.ts checks each committed report under packages/library-types/fidelity/authored/ and fidelity/native/ against a fresh measurement of the vendored copy. After re-vendoring, re-run bun run --cwd packages/library-types parity, review the coverage change, and commit the reports in the same commit. An upstream change that moves no number leaves the reports as they are. The provenance assertions. The toolchain's api-surface-loader.test.ts reads the pin back out of the emitted API-doc metadata and asserts it exactly — for druid, meta.commit is the ref in druid/reviewed.json and meta.sourceUrl is https://github.com/Insality/druid/tree/<ref>. A bump moves both, and they are in a different package from the pin you edited. The pin kind. refKind in the library's library.json says whether the pin is a release, a tag or a commit, and the docs page's adopt step follows it. It moves with the pin: api-surface-loader.test.ts reds when the asset-portal register records another kind at the same ref. The pin-refresh record. packages/library-types/pin-refresh.json states which members a bump added and removed, one entry per refresh, each tagged with the lane it belongs to (luals, script-api, or openapi). packages/cli/src/library/pin-refresh.test.ts checks every name it states against the surface that lane's own parser yields for the committed fixtures — buildTargetModel, committedScriptApiDoc, or parseOpenApi. Regenerating the fixtures without updating the record reds ci, so derive the new entry by diffing the old and new member names rather than from upstream release notes. A second key, deliberatelyUnmoved, records a pin you examined and chose to leave alone, and is guarded on its ref alone — so a note left standing after that pin later moves also reds. The guard deliberately does not check that the record is complete, nor its changedMembers and notes, which are prose. The compile-only surface proofs. The .test-d.ts files under each library folder's usage/ assert the emitted .d.ts by assigning from it, and pin the absence of non-public members with @ts-expect-error. A bump breaks them in both directions: a member that left the public surface fails the assignment, and a member upstream stopped marking @field private or @local makes its expect-error directive unused (TS2578). The second is the easy one to misread — check the old and new fixture annotations before assuming the emitter regressed, because dropping a private marker upstream is a real surface change and the declaration is then correct to emit. The generated docs artifacts. packages/docs/llms.txt, packages/docs/llms-full.txt, and the docs-site search and symbol indexes are committed, not built on demand. Regenerate them with bun run --cwd packages/docs-site build-indexes whenever the API-doc model changed.

on_viewable_change(fn: (viewable: boolean) => void): () => void Calls fn each time the game's viewability changes, starting from its value at subscribe time, and returns a function that unsubscribes fn. Lua polls the value every 0.25 s, so a change arrives up to about 250 ms late. Subscribing the same fn again returns its existing unsubscribe, and unsubscribing twice is safe. An error fn raises is printed and does not stop the other subscribers. The poll runs on a timer that belongs to the script that subscribed last and stops with it, so subscribe from a script that outlives the subscription and unsubscribe in its final. Outside an HTML5 build fn is never called and the returned function does nothing. fn — Gets true when the game becomes viewable and false when it stops.

playables.on_audio_enabled_change(callback: function | nil) Registers a callback for YouTube audio-setting changes. Before the callback runs, the extension automatically mutes the master sound group when audio is disabled, or unmutes it when audio is enabled and the game is not paused. A new callback replaces the previous one. Pass nil to unregister it. This function cannot be called from its own callback. callback — The event callback, or nil to unregister the current callback.

playables.on_pause(callback: function | nil) Registers a callback for YouTube pause events. The extension automatically mutes the master sound group before the callback runs. A new callback replaces the previous one. Pass nil to unregister it. This function cannot be called from its own callback. A paused game is not guaranteed to resume. callback — The event callback, or nil to unregister the current callback.

playables.on_resume(callback: function | nil) Registers a callback for YouTube resume events. Before the callback runs, the extension automatically unmutes the master sound group if YouTube audio is enabled, or keeps it muted if audio is disabled. A new callback replaces the previous one. Pass nil to unregister it. This function cannot be called from its own callback. callback — The event callback, or nil to unregister the current callback.

The content type is optional and defaults to CONTENT_TYPE_VIDEO. Only one request may be in progress at a time. The request remains in progress until its callback returns, so the callback cannot start another open_yt_content() request. content_id — The YouTube video or Playable ID. content_type — CONTENT_TYPE_VIDEO or CONTENT_TYPE_PLAYABLE.

playables.request_interstitial_ad(callback: function) Requests an interstitial ad. Success does not guarantee that an ad was shown. Do not use this API to grant rewards. Only one interstitial request may be in progress at a time. The request remains in progress until its callback returns, so the callback cannot start another request_interstitial_ad() request. Keep handling YouTube audio, pause, and resume events during ads.

playables.request_rewarded_ad(reward_id: string, callback: function) Requests a rewarded ad. Grant a reward only when reward_earned is true. Only one rewarded request may be in progress at a time. The request remains in progress until its callback returns, so the callback cannot start another request_rewarded_ad() request. Keep handling YouTube audio, pause, and resume events during ads. reward_id — A stable ID unique to the reward type. Reuse it for each offer of that reward and do not include user data.

playables.save_data(data: string, callback: function) Saves valid UTF-8 text to YouTube, with a maximum size of 3 MiB. Invalid UTF-8 returns false and an error through the callback before the SDK is called. Base64-encode binary data such as sys.serialize() output before saving. Only one save request may be in progress at a time. The request remains in progress until its callback returns, so the callback cannot start another save_data() request. data — The serialized game data as valid UTF-8 text. Embedded zero bytes are supported.

playables.send_score(score: number, callback: function) Sends an integer score to YouTube. Use one consistent score dimension across the game. Only one request may be in progress at a time. The request remains in progress until its callback returns, so the callback cannot start another send_score() request. score — An integer no greater than JavaScript's maximum safe integer.

Put the authored/forked declaration at the authored path. For a fork of a ts-defold binding, that is the ts-defold lane's codemodded output (codemodDeclaration in packages/cli/src/library/sync-library-types.ts) — not the raw ts-defold fixture, which the ts-defold lane type-maps on the way out (hash/url/vmath.vector3 → Hash/Url/Vector3) while the authored lane emits its input verbatim, so forking the fixture would ship upstream's Lua type names and fail the dts-declaration-validity gate. The two forms coincide when the library references no mapped core types (persist), which is why the rule is safe to state unconditionally. For a hand-authored library, it is the declaration you wrote. Either way it must be a declare module '<moduleId>' ambient — the target form the emit passes through unchanged. When the library is a native extension, the declaration also carries / @globalTable / so project imports lower to its runtime global rather than a require (see Module form). Then run this command from the toolchain root: resolve serves the vendored .d.ts with one change: each member upstream documents carries upstream's LuaDoc summary as its doc comment unless the fork's own comment is pinned to that text (see Upstream LuaDoc import). Nothing else is transformed: an authored source is already target-form, so the served types are the vendored types. --api-doc-out makes library check, once its checks pass, run extractApiDoc over that printed declaration under the pinned publish namespace, producing the api-doc/<namespace>.json the /api page renders. A member's @deprecated tag carries through to the page as a Deprecated line, with the tag's own text when it has any — so mark a deprecated member in the fork rather than only saying so in its prose. There is no fetch command — the source is vendored by hand, not snapshotted from a primary source — and no fidelity command: there is no primary source to compare against, and the emit is lossless by construction (see below).

Reach this lane only after ruling out the generated ones. Ask, in order: Does upstream ship a .script_api? → it is a script_api target. Does its Lua carry inline ---@ annotations? → it is a LuaLS target. Does its README document the full surface precisely? → it may be a markdown target (gated on a fidelity comparison; a lossy README is a no-go and the library does not regenerate from markdown). None of the above → it is an authored target, and you choose between fork, hand-author, and keep. A markdown no-go is a verdict on the markdown source, not on the ts-defold dependency. It says the README cannot regenerate the surface; it says nothing about where the surface should be maintained. That second question is this lane's, and a no-go library reaches question 4 with it still open — so run the cost model below on it exactly as you would on a library that never had a README at all. keep is a legitimate answer, but it has to be chosen, not inherited from the refusal. persist.persist and orthographic.camera are the worked examples.

Record a parityVerdict instead of an empty upstreamLua. The reason comes from a closed set — an unknown one throws, naming the entry — and the note must say what was actually looked at: | reason | When it applies | | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | unresolved-path | The moduleId-derived path does not resolve at the pinned ref, including a repository that no longer exists there. No corpus target carries this verdict. Before recording it, check whether the upstream merely moved — an account rename usually redirects, and the same history may be reachable under a new owner. If it is genuinely gone, prefer dropping the library over shipping types nobody can obtain a runtime for. | | reason | When it applies | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | no-module-file | Upstream resolves, but declares no single module file this target could be measured against. | | reason | When it applies | | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | unparseable-shape | The module file exists but closes in a way the reader refuses — a metatable carrying index, or one it cannot read the keys of, either of which could delegate members no column-0 scan would find. No corpus target carries this verdict: boom.boom and in.accelerometer once did, and were lifted into measurement when the reader learned the return setmetatable(M, { call = … }) form they close with. | A verdict is a recorded finding, not a way to skip the work. It says someone looked and what stopped them, which is exactly what an absent declaration cannot say. The corpus currently carries no verdict of any kind — all 35 targets are measured — so every reason above is described rather than exemplified.

register(type_name: string, def: LuaTable): LuaTable Register a custom element type definition. Every element type string ("box", "text", "button", etc.) must be registered before it can appear in a UI tree. The definition describes how to create, update, and interact with the corresponding Defold GUI node. Required fields in def: create_node(el) -> userdata — creates and returns a new gui node Optional fields in def: apply(self, el, node, alpha) — update node visuals each frame is_visible(el) -> boolean — custom visibility check is_hittable(el) -> boolean — custom hit-test eligibility is_scroll_container -> boolean — marks element as scroll root clips_children -> boolean — node is used as parent for children capture_descendant_hits -> boolean — returns self instead of child on hit is_backdrop_click_target -> boolean — receives backdrop click events get_text_anchor(el) -> "left"|"center"|"right" — text pivot anchor for positioning hover_begin(self, el, deps) — called when pointer enters element hover_end(self, el, deps) — called when pointer leaves element press_begin(self, el, deps) — called when element is pressed press_update(self, el, is_hot, deps) — called while dragging over element press_end(self, el, activated, deps) — called on release on_wheel(self, el, delta, deps) — called on mouse wheel on_drag_start(self, el, x, y, t, deps) — called when drag begins on_drag_move(self, el, x, y, t, deps) — called each drag frame on_drag_end(self, el, action, t, deps) — called when drag ends update_anim(el, dt, deps) -> bool,bool — per-frame animation tick render_extras(self, el, prefix, alpha, deps) — render auxiliary nodes collect_extra_keys(el, prefix, keys, deps) — declare extra cached node keys get_child_extra_offset_y(el) -> number — additional Y offset for children type_name — The element type string (e.g. "box", "scroll") def — Renderer definition table; must contain create_node The registered def, same reference as the argument

rnd.boolean(id: number): boolean Returns true or false with equal probability. id — RNG context id. Random Boolean — Random boolean value.

rnd.bound(id: number, upper_bound: number): number Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer in [0, upper_bound). id — RNG context id. upper_bound — Exclusive upper bound. Must be an unsigned 32-bit integer greater than 0. Random Number — Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer in [0, upper_bound).
rnd.card(id: number): number Picks a standard deck card index. id — RNG context id. Card — Card index in [1, 52]. ⚠️ 1-based; passed to random unchanged.
rnd.card2(id: number): LuaMultiReturn<[number, number]> Picks a standard deck suit and rank. id — RNG context id. Suit — Suit in [1, 4]. Card — Card rank in [1, 13].

rnd.chance(id: number, probability: number): boolean Returns true according to the given probability. id — RNG context id. probability — Probability from 0.0 to 1.0. Values <= 0 are always false and values >= 1 are always true. Success — True if the probability check succeeds.
rnd.check(id: number) Debug/sample method that prints PCG sample output and consumes RNG state. id — RNG context id.
rnd.clear_contexts() Deletes all RNG contexts. Existing context ids become invalid.
rnd.delete(id: number) Deletes an RNG context. The context id becomes invalid. id — RNG context id.

rnd.dice(id: number, roll: number, type: number): LuaMultiReturn<[table, number]> Rolls dice using one of the exported dice constants. id — RNG context id. roll — Roll count. Must be greater than 0. type — Dice type. Use rnd.d4, rnd.d6, rnd.d8, rnd.d10, rnd.d12, rnd.d20, or rnd.d100. Results — Table of dice results. Total — Total amount of dice results.

rnd.double_range(id: number, min: number, max: number): number Returns a floating point number in [min, max). Not fast as rnd.double(id) id — RNG context id. min — Minimum number. max — Maximum number. Random Number — Returns a floating point number in [min, max).
rnd.double(id: number): number Returns a floating point number in [0, 1). id — RNG context id. Random Number — Returns a floating point number in [0, 1).

rnd.doubles(id: number, count: number): table Returns a table of floating point numbers in [0, 1). id — RNG context id. count — Number of values to generate. Must be a non-negative integer. Random Numbers — Table of floating point numbers in [0, 1).

rnd.new(init_state: number, init_seq: number): number Creates an isolated RNG context and returns its context id. Call without arguments to seed from entropy, with init_state to use init_seq = 1, or with init_state and init_seq for exact unsigned 32-bit deterministic seeding. init_state — Optional starting state for the RNG. Must be an unsigned 32-bit integer. init_seq — Optional output sequence for the RNG. Must be an unsigned 32-bit integer. Id — RNG context id.

rnd.new64(init_state: string, init_seq: string): number Creates an isolated RNG context using exact unsigned 64-bit decimal string seeds. init_state — Starting state for the RNG as an unsigned 64-bit decimal string. init_seq — Output sequence for the RNG as an unsigned 64-bit decimal string. Id — RNG context id.
rnd.number(id: number): number Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer. id — RNG context id. Random Number — Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer.

rnd.numbers(id: number, count: number): table Returns a table of 32-bit unsigned integers. id — RNG context id. count — Number of values to generate. Must be a non-negative integer. Random Numbers — Table of 32-bit unsigned integers.

rnd.pcg32(init_state: number, init_seq: number) Creates a pcg32 instance. Can specify init_state and init_seq to start with a seed, or nothing to get a random one init_state — init_state is the starting state for the PCG32, you can pass any 64-bit value. init_seq — init_seq selects the output sequence for the PCG32, you can pass any 64-bit value, although only the low 63 bits are significant.

rnd.range(id: number, min: number, max: number): number Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer between min and max values, inclusive. Only unsigned integers are supported. id — RNG context id. min — Minimum unsigned integer. max — Maximum unsigned integer. Random Number — Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer between min and max values.

rnd.ranges(id: number, count: number, min: number, max: number): table Returns a table of 32-bit unsigned integers between min and max values, inclusive. id — RNG context id. count — Number of values to generate. Must be a non-negative integer. min — Minimum unsigned integer. max — Maximum unsigned integer. Random Numbers — Table of 32-bit unsigned integers between min and max values.

rnd.reset(id: number, init_state: number, init_seq: number) Reseeds an existing RNG context. Call with only id to seed from entropy, with id and init_state to use init_seq = 1, or with id, init_state, and init_seq for exact unsigned 32-bit deterministic seeding. id — RNG context id. init_state — Optional starting state for the RNG. Must be an unsigned 32-bit integer. init_seq — Optional output sequence for the RNG. Must be an unsigned 32-bit integer.

rnd.reset64(id: number, init_state: string, init_seq: string) Reseeds an existing RNG context using exact unsigned 64-bit decimal string seeds. id — RNG context id. init_state — Starting state for the RNG as an unsigned 64-bit decimal string. init_seq — Output sequence for the RNG as an unsigned 64-bit decimal string.
rnd.roll(id: number): number Roll the dice. id — RNG context id. Random Number — Returns between 1-6

rnd.shuffle(id: number, array: table): table Shuffles the array part of a table in place using Fisher-Yates. id — RNG context id. array — Table to shuffle. Array — The same table, shuffled in place.

rnd.state(id: number): LuaMultiReturn<[string, string]> Returns raw PCG state and increment as unsigned 64-bit decimal strings. id — RNG context id. State — Raw PCG state. Increment — Raw PCG increment. Controls the PCG stream.

rng: (this: void, x: number, y: number) => number The number generator Random and RandomWithChances draw with.

roll_custom_dice(num_dice: number, sides: Array<[ number, number ]>): number Roll custom dice. rtcapture.cancel_all(): number Drop every pending capture request. No callbacks are invoked. count — How many requests were dropped.

rtcapture.cancel(request_id: number): boolean Drop a pending capture request. Its callback is never invoked, because cancelling was the caller's own decision. Everything the request owned is released immediately. request_id — The id returned by capture. cancelled — True when a pending request with that id was found and removed.

rtcapture.capture_sync(target: number, options: table): LuaMultiReturn<[table, string, string]> Read the given target immediately instead of waiting for post render. Takes the same options as capture and returns the same result table, only as a direct return value. Use it where no further post render will happen - the save written from the final() of a game script when the window is closing is the case this exists for, since a queued request there would never run. A render target still has to be captured from the render script that owns it and in the frame it was drawn; the screen framebuffer can be captured from anywhere. target — The value returned by render.render_target(), or rtcapture.RENDER_TARGET_DEFAULT. options — The same options capture accepts. result — The same result table capture passes to its callback, or nil when the request was rejected outright. error — Error code when the request was rejected, otherwise nil. message — Human readable reason when the request was rejected, otherwise nil.

rtcapture.capture(target: number, options: table, callback: function): LuaMultiReturn<[number, string, string]> Queue a readback of the given render target. The readback runs in the post-render phase of the current frame, so call this from the render script that owns the target and in the same frame the target was drawn. The extension does not own the target and cannot detect that it was deleted or resized after the request. target — The value returned by render.render_target(), or rtcapture.RENDER_TARGET_DEFAULT for the main screen framebuffer. The screen can be captured from any script; a render target must come from the render script that owns it. options — format - "raw" (default) for pixels in a Defold buffer, "hold" to keep the pixels inside the extension and get a frame_id for encode, "png" or "jpeg". Use "hold" to spread a capture over two frames: the frame that reads pays for the readback only, and the downscale and the encoding happen on the next frame, without a multi megabyte buffer travelling through Lua in between. max_width - target width of the resulting image. The extension picks the integer box filter factor itself, because only it knows the size of the region it read. Rounding is down, with a minimum of 1, so the result can be slightly wider than asked: 3840 with max_width = 600 gives 640. Without this option the image keeps the size of the region that was read. path - encoded formats only. When given, the image is written to that file and is not copied into a Lua string. The file is written through path .. ".tmp" and only then replaces the destination. channels - 4 for RGBA8 or 3 for RGB8 with alpha discarded. Defaults to 4, or to 3 for JPEG, which cannot store alpha anyway. PNG keeps alpha losslessly for four channels and writes a true 24bpp PNG for three. quality - JPEG only, 1..100, default 85. subsampling - JPEG only, "444", "422" or "420", default "420". Use "444" for text and interface, where chroma subsampling produces coloured fringes. progressive - JPEG only, default false. Encodes noticeably slower and decodes slower, with little size benefit for local previews. optimize - JPEG only, default false. Optimized Huffman tables cost encoding time. alpha_mode - JPEG from four channels. "discard" (default) ignores alpha, so transparent areas keep whatever colour they hold. "composite" blends onto background first. background - table with r, g, b in 0..255, used by alpha_mode = "composite". Defaults to black. x, y, width, height - rectangle to read, with the origin in the top left corner of the target, matching the orientation of the returned image. x and y default to 0; width and height default to the rest of the target. A rectangle that leaves the target is rejected, never clamped. flip_y - flip rows vertically, false by default. The default was measured: on the OpenGL adapter ReadPixels already returns top-down rows. tag - any Lua value, returned unchanged in the result so a caller can correlate the result with its own request. callback — Called from post-render with one result table. request_id — Monotonic id of the accepted request, or nil when the request was rejected. error — Error code when the request was rejected, otherwise nil. message — Human readable reason when the request was rejected, otherwise nil.

rtcapture.debug_target(target: number, label?: string): table Identify an arbitrary render target without reading its pixels. Call it from the render script that owns the target, in the same frame, so the handle is guaranteed to be alive. target — The value returned by render.render_target(). label — Name used in the log line so several targets can be told apart. info — Contains label, handle, handle_hex, color0_width, color0_height and adapter.

rtcapture.decode_jpeg(data: string, options?: table): LuaMultiReturn<[table, string, string]> Decode JPEG bytes into a Defold buffer. Synchronous, and callable from any script. The header is validated before anything is allocated dimensions, data precision and colour space are checked first, and images above 64 million pixels are refused. JPEG stores no alpha, so a four channel result is always fully opaque. data — Binary JPEG data. options — channels - 4 for RGBA8 (default) or 3 for RGB8. image — Contains width, height, channels, byte_size, decode_ms and buffer, a Defold buffer whose single stream is rgba of UINT8 x4, or rgb of UINT8 x3. nil when decoding failed. error — Error code when decoding failed, otherwise nil. message — Human readable reason when decoding failed, otherwise nil.

rtcapture.encode(frame_id: number, options: table): LuaMultiReturn<[table, string, string]> Downscale and encode a frame that a format = "hold" capture left inside the extension. This is the second phase of a capture spread over two frames. The frame stays held after encoding, so the same shot can be encoded more than once - to compare formats, for example - and is freed by release_frame. Compositing is not available here the held pixels have already been converted, so alpha_mode = "composite" only works at capture time. frame_id — The frame_id from the result of the held capture. options — format (required, "png" or "jpeg"), path, max_width, quality, subsampling, progressive, optimize and tag - the same meaning they have in capture. result — The same result table shape as capture, with downscale_ms, encode_ms, write_ms and total_ms filled for this phase. nil when the call was rejected. error — ERR_NO_HELD_FRAME when no frame with that id is held, otherwise nil. message — Human readable reason when the call was rejected, otherwise nil.

rtcapture.get_capabilities(): table Report what the extension can currently do on the installed graphics adapter. Only verified capabilities are listed; stages that are not implemented yet do not appear as fields. capabilities — Contains available, adapter ("opengl", "vulkan", "directx", ...) and debug_target.

rtcapture.get_render_target_size(target: number): LuaMultiReturn<[number, number]> Report the size of the COLOR0 attachment of the given render target, so calling code can compute a rectangle without repeating the parameters the render script created the target with. target — The value returned by render.render_target().

rtcapture.invalidate_render_targets(): number Declare that every render target handed to the extension so far is gone. Call this right after recreating render targets, for example when the window was resized. The extension cannot detect this on its own - the public DMSDK has no way to test whether a handle is still alive. Requests made before the call stay in the queue and complete with ERR_RENDER_TARGET_DESTROYED rather than reading through a dead handle, so every accepted request still gets exactly one answer. Requests for rtcapture.RENDER_TARGET_DEFAULT are unaffected. affected — How many pending requests will now fail.

rtcapture.release_frame(frame_id?: number): boolean Free the frame held by a format = "hold" capture. Call it once the frame has been encoded, or when the encoding is abandoned - otherwise a full screen frame stays in the memory of the extension until the next held capture replaces it. Only one frame is held at a time. frame_id — The id to free. Without it the currently held frame is freed, whatever its id. released — True when a frame was actually freed.

rtcapture.RENDER_TARGET_DEFAULT Pass as the capture target to read the main screen framebuffer instead of a render target. Its value is 0, the same one render.RENDER_TARGET_DEFAULT uses in a render script.

rtcapture.set_debug_logging(enabled: boolean) Enable the detailed capture log. Off by default. The log line reports the raw first pixel before conversion, the viewport before and after the readback, and per stage timings.

Run library check over the library data. It runs the reader's checks, prints every module, and type-checks every module resolve prints under skipLibCheck: false, together with each library folder's usage/ examples, so a new target is compiled as soon as its recipe.json lists it; the dts-declaration-validity test runs the same check. Fidelity parity is gated per namespace. Then run the library tests: A brand-new library has no floor entry yet, and the floor gate fails until it gets one — fidelity-floor.ts --raise seeds it at the coverage you just measured. Commit the library's library.json with its floor, reviewed.json and recipe.json and the snapshotted source/<namespace>/ together. Both emitted report folders (fidelity/, api-doc/) are gitignored here and stay uncommitted.

Run the three commands from the toolchain root, in order. Each iterates every LuaLS target in library data, so an unchanged entry re-emits byte-for-byte and only your new entry produces new files. --fetch reads the pinned tree, applies sourceGlobs minus ignore, and writes each selected .lua under <library>/source/<namespace>/, preserving tree shape. This is the only command that touches the network; everything after it reads those committed fixtures, so the pipeline is reproducible offline. --fidelity parses the fixtures and reports how much of the surface resolved to a known type (see below). resolve prints the .d.ts a consumer sees from these fixtures, or from the dependency's own archive. Interfaces and aliases come from the whole snapshot; the module's own functions come only from the moduleId file. --api-doc-out makes library check lower the same model, once its checks pass, to the JSON the /api page renders. A ---@deprecated before a ---@class, ---@alias, or a function declaration carries into both artifacts — as a JSDoc @deprecated in the .d.ts and as a Deprecated line on the /api page, with the tag's own text when it has any. A tag on a type still reaches only the .d.ts, since a type has no page heading of its own to carry the line. Only the strict ---@deprecated form is read; a spaced --- @deprecated is treated as prose, as it is for every other tag.

set_migrations(migrations_table: ((game_state: saver_game_state, logger: saver_logger) => undefined)[]) Sets the list of migrations to apply after loading the game state manually with saver.apply_migrations() function. Migrations are used to update the game state in case of changes to the game state structure. Migrations are applied in order. Each migration should be a function that takes the game state as a parameter and returns the updated game state. local migrations = { -- Migration 1 function(game_state, logger) -- Assume we have new level_data field in the game state and we need to move level and score to it game_state.game.level_data = { level = game_state.game.level, score = game_state.game.score } game_state.game.level = nil game_state.game.score = nil return game_state }, -- Migration 2 function(game_state, logger) -- Just an example, multiply the score by 1000. For example we changed our score system game_state.game.level_data.score = game_state.game.level_data.score 1000 return game_state } } saver.set_migrations(migrations) saver.init() saver.bind_save_state("game", game_state) saver.apply_migrations() migrations_table — Array of migration functions

Severing ts-defold for the library is the same single-module cutover the generated lanes use: Drop the library's row from library-targets.json and its dir from library-classification.json, and delete the retired fixtures/ts-defold/<moduleId>.d.ts. Its api-doc/<moduleId>.json golden is deleted only when the fork publishes under a different namespace; when namespace === moduleId it is instead overwritten in place by the command above. The namespace now resolves to your authored artifacts. Add a usage/<library>-usage.test-d.ts compile proof in the library folder, moving any hand-written block for the old dotted specifier into it. library check type-checks every .ts file under a library's usage/ under skipLibCheck: false together with every module resolve prints, the fork among them. The ts-defold registry is now empty: every library it once carried has severed, so library-targets.json holds "targets": []. The file stays committed anyway — the CLI's registry loader treats a missing file as "no vendored libraries at all" and would drop the LuaLS, script_api and authored lanes with it, and library-classification.json pins its commit against that source block. The site's fourth maintainedHere loader reads each library's forks, so the namespace becomes authored-here — absent from the ts-defold classification and present in a first-party corpus — and its /api page carries the upstream pin automatically. Then run the gates: Commit the library's library.json and reviewed.json, the vendored fork/<moduleId>.d.ts and its usage/ examples together, along with the config and manifest deletions. The emitted api-doc/ report folder is gitignored here and stays uncommitted.

This would be the case if doing a show() from a popup on the screen just below the popup. sequential - Set to true to wait for the previous screen to show itself out before starting the show in transition even when transitioning to a different scene ID. no_stack - Set to true to load the screen without adding it to the screen stack. pop - The number of screens to pop from the stack before adding the new one. data — Optional data to set on the screen. Some Defold libraries ship no usable structured type source — no .script_api, no inline LuaLS (---@) annotations, and no README that documents the surface precisely enough to parse. The LuaLS, .script_api, and markdown front-ends all ingest a primary source and generate a declaration; a library with none of those has nothing to generate from. Its .d.ts must be written by hand — either forked from an existing hand-authored declaration or authored fresh — and vendored into the library's folder in the toolchain repo as first-party source. resolve then prints the vendored declaration into the consumer's project, the way it prints the generated lanes' declarations. Like the other lanes, adding such a library is data, not code: you add one fork to the library's library.json in its folder, packages/library-types/data/<version>/<host>/<owner>/<repo>/ (the newest version-named folder), vendor the .d.ts into the folder's fork/, run the generation command, and commit the library's files. Every path a fork names is relative to the library folder, except apiDoc and fidelity, which are relative to packages/library-types/, where the tools write their reports. The toolchain's authored front-end (packages/cli/src/library/sync-authored-types.ts) is the reusable machinery; you touch config and fixtures, not the pipeline. This page is for library-type authors. Library data lives in the toolchain repo under packages/library-types/data/, so you add or change a library with a pull request there, not to defold-typescript/library-data. If you only want to use a vendored library in your own game, you need nothing here — just declare the dependency and run resolve. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root. Each tool reads and writes the library data under packages/library-types/data/ and writes its reports to api-doc/ and fidelity/ in packages/library-types/.

Some divergences are not defects. When upstream's own source says a member is not for consumers, declaring it would widen the published surface with a function nobody should call — so the fork is right to omit it, and the report should say so rather than charge it as a gap. parityExceptions in the library's library.json is where that is recorded. It maps each fork's namespace to an array of { name, kind, reason } entries sorted by name. An excepted member counts as correct, is absent from missingMembers, and appears in the artifact's parityExceptions carrying its reason — so a target that reached 1 by justification reads differently from one that reached 1 by declaring everything. kind is a closed set, in the same shape as parityVerdict's reason: | kind | When it applies | | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | script-lifecycle | Upstream exports the member for the library's own bundled .script and says so in its own comment. boom's five hooks carry -- called from boom.script; orthographic.camera's init, final and update say "called automatically from … the camera.script" in LuaDoc. | | kind | When it applies | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | deprecated-stub | Upstream's body is nothing but error("… is deprecated"), so the member cannot succeed if called. orthographic.camera keeps ten such one-line stubs; six are excepted here. | reason must cite upstream's file and line, so the entry can be re-checked against the pin instead of taken on trust. An arity or phantom exception is deliberately not expressible — no kind is added before a real case asks for one. An entry cannot outlive the defect it justifies. Three throws enforce that, each naming the offending entry: an unknown kind, rejected at parse time; an entry naming a member the pinned upstream does not define — the member was renamed or removed, and the entry is stale; an entry for a member the fork does declare — the exception is unnecessary and must be deleted rather than left to rot. The ledger is not a way to skip a correction. It is the other half of correct it or justify it, and every entry is a claim about upstream that the next reader can check.

Some pure-Lua Defold libraries ship their own type information as inline LuaLS (---@) annotations rather than a .script_api. This toolchain prints TypeScript declarations for them from those annotations, so a consumer that declares the library gets autocomplete and tsc coverage with no hand-written .d.ts. resolve prints the declaration into the consumer's project from the library version it depends on, or from the sources pinned in library data. Adding such a library is data, not code: you add one entry to the luals list of the library's recipe.json, in its folder under the library data folder (the newest version-named folder under packages/library-types/data/; the library folder also holds the fetched sources under source/), run the three generation commands, check the emitted API-doc description, and commit the library's files and its artifacts. There is no pipeline source to touch — the same front-end that produces the druid types produces yours. This page is for library-type authors. Library data lives in the toolchain repo under packages/library-types/data/, so you add or change a library with a pull request there, not to defold-typescript/library-data. If you only want to use a vendored library in your own game, you need nothing here — just declare the dependency and run resolve. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root. Each tool reads and writes the library data under packages/library-types/data/ and writes its reports to api-doc/ and fidelity/ in packages/library-types/.

Some tokens belong to no target at all — the ambient Lua standard library already declares them. log's ---@param debuginfo debuginfo names the table debug.getinfo() returns, which lua-types types as debug.FunctionInfo. That takes a typeRenames entry, not an externalTypes one: The emitted signature reads debuginfo: debug.FunctionInfo with no import line, and the log page renders that same dotted name — the way Vector3 and Opaque<"node"> already render there. The rule: a token another target owns takes externalTypes and gets an import; a token the ambient stdlib already declares takes a dotted typeRenames value and gets none. A library that declares the token itself wins over either, so a rename never shadows a real local declaration. Two naming rules keep such a local declaration from hiding the type a rename names, and both apply with no configuration. An alias that names itself in its own body means the type it shadows: ---@alias hash userdata|hash emits type hash = Opaque<"userdata"> | Hash, and every other hash in the library still names the local alias. A declaration named like a core or typeRenames value is declared with a trailing underscore: ---@alias Url url|string emits type Url = Url | string, the library's own Url references read Url, and an engine url still reads Url. Two declarations that land on one generated name, such as Url beside the library's own Url, fail the emit naming both. Where an upstream annotation restates a member it inherits from such a parent, and restates it incompatibly enough that the emitted redeclaration would not type-check, drop the restatement with an annotationOverrides field override — "fields": { "subscribe": { "drop": true } } — and let the member inherit. Like every override, a drop naming an absent field throws rather than passing silently. The second drop shape is a class-level @overload. The emitter lowers one onto the interface as a call signature, which is right whenever the class really is callable — event's EVENT_METATABLE and PROMISE_METATABLE each carry a real call. It is wrong where the @overload describes the module table while the interface types the instance: log reuses one table as both, but only the module table gets call, and get_logger returns an instance built on { index = M }, which Lua never treats as callable. Drop that signature with "callSignature": { "drop": true } on the interface. Same loud failure as the others: an override naming an interface that has no call signature throws. Some libraries bind a ---@class to a field of the module table instead of declaring a ---@field for it: token writes ---@class token.event.on_token_change: event directly above M.on_token_change = event.create(). The class becomes an interface, but nothing exports the value, so token.on_token_change would not exist in TypeScript. A moduleObject override names the module's class and each bound field with its class: Each field emits as export const on_token_change: token_event_on_token_change;, documented with its class's description, and the module's own class is no longer emitted as an empty interface. The override throws when the module class or a field's type is absent from the model, when the module class already declares the field (upstream added the ---@field, so delete the entry), when a module function has the same name, and when the parser already treats a different class as the module object. Other libraries assign constants to the module table with no annotation at all: live-unbundler writes M.MSG_ALL_LOADED = hash("all_loaded") and M.RES_BOTH = 3 at the top of its module file, so the lane exports neither. A moduleConstants override types each one with a LuaLS token and an optional doc line: Each entry emits as a documented export const MSG_ALL_LOADED: Hash; and appears on the /api page, and its token counts toward the fidelity report like any annotation. Only a column-0 M.NAME = ... on the table the module's own file returns (return M) counts as an assignment, as does the first target of M.DEBUG, M[1] = 1, "DEBUG"; an assignment on another table, such as Other.NAME = 1, does not. The override throws when the returned table never has the name assigned at column 0, when a module function has the same name, and when the module object's class already declares it as a field. A ---@meta file can describe a class's functions with dot syntax: ads-wrapper's ads_networks/ads_network.lua starts with ---@meta, puts ---@class ads_network on local ads_network = { NAME = "ads_network" }, and then annotates function ads_network.setup(params) and its siblings. When the tag is the file's first non-blank line, each such function becomes a method of ads_network declared with this: void (setup(this: void, params?: unknown | undefined): void;), because callers invoke it as network.setup(params), not network:setup(params). In any other file the same form stays a module function, since a runtime module may annotate its own table as a class and still export its functions. A dot function on another local table belongs to that table when the returned module re-exports it at column 0. flow's flow/flex.lua defines function Node.new(opts) on local Node = {}, assigns FL.Node = Node, and ends with return FL, so new is declared on export const Node: { "new"(this: void, ...): Node }, not as a top-level flex.new. Because the file also sets Node.index = Node and Node.new declares ---@return Flow.FlexNode, the Node interface extends Flow_FlexNode, and new plus every method annotated ---@return Flow.FlexNode self return Node, so flex.Node.new({ key: "root" }).set_width(960).calculate_layout(960, 640) keeps the chainable methods. A table exported under several fields is declared under each field. A field assigned more than once declares the table it is assigned last. Where an annotation types a parameter wrongly, a type token on a moduleFunctions parameter replaces it: ads-wrapper's queue.lua writes ---@param fn ads_callback, though run calls fn(network, callback, params), so the ads_wrapper.queue target retypes it: add then emits fn: (network: ads_network, callback: ads_callback, params?: LuaTable) => void. A parameter of interfaces.<name>.methods.<method>.params takes the same type key. Naming an absent function or parameter throws. "optional": true on interfaces.<name>.methods.<method> emits the method as name?(...), for a method the library checks for before it calls it. ads-wrapper's wrapper.lua guards the call with if network.request_idfa then, so the ads_wrapper targets mark ads_network.request_idfa optional, and a network without it still passes ads_wrapper.ads_wrapper.register_network.
