Start with library add, which writes the folder below from the archive URL, with a starting luals entry and the sources it reads: Then edit recipe.json by hand: add typeRenames and externalTypes for the tokens the library's annotations leave unmapped, narrow sourceGlobs and ignore, and add an entry for each other module the library exposes. The tables below describe every field. Each library pins its own repository and tag — a LuaLS library ships no .d.ts, only annotations, and each lives in its own repo at its own release. Its folder is named for the repository: its <host>/<owner>/<repo>, lowercased, without .git (https://github.com/Insality/druid is github.com/insality/druid/). The folder pins the library once: | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | ------ | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | repo | yes | The GitHub repository URL, e.g. https://github.com/Insality/druid. | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | license | no | SPDX-style license id, surfaced by the library page's provenance block. Defaults to "". | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | refKind | no | "tag" or "commit" when upstream publishes no stable release (GitHub's latest release skips prereleases), so the docs page's adopt step names the pinned archive instead of linking a releases page. Omit it for a repo with releases. | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | --------------- | ----- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | reviewed.json | ref | yes | The exact release tag to pin. Resolve the newest stable tag (git ls-remote --tags <repo>) — never invent one. | Each generated module is one entry in recipe.json's luals list: | Field | Required | What it is | | ------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | sourceGlobs | yes | Globs selecting the .lua files to snapshot, relative to the repo root (e.g. ["druid//.lua"]). | | Field | Required | What it is | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | moduleId | yes | The library's runtime require path, dotted (e.g. druid.druid). This names the emitted declare module and scopes the module-function surface to <moduleId-as-path>.lua. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ----------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | namespace | yes | The artifact stem — the emitted files are fidelity/<namespace>.json and api-doc/<namespace>.json. The fetched sources sit under the library folder's source/<namespace>/. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | typeRenames | no | Map from a LuaLS type name to the TypeScript type text to emit (e.g. { "vector3": "Vector3" }). The value is emitted verbatim and may name an ambient global, including a dotted one like debug.FunctionInfo — it never contributes an import. Omit or {} when the library references no renamed types. | | Field | Required | What it is | | -------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | ignore | no | Globs excluded from sourceGlobs — tests, examples, editor widgets. Defaults to []. | | Field | Required | What it is | | --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | externalTypes | no | Map from a type name another target owns to { "module": "<its moduleId>", "name": "<its export>" } — see below. Omit when the library references no other library's types. | A missing required field fails loudly, naming the field, the offending entry and its recipe.json.

Start with library add, which writes the folder, library.json and reviewed.json from the archive URL: Then add the forks entry to library.json by hand, and vendor the upstream Lua it measures against. library add writes no fork, and when it wrote a recipe.json for a generated module, delete that entry and its source/ files if the fork replaces it. Each library sits in its own folder under the data folder, named for its repository: the URL's last path segment, lowercased, without .git (https://github.com/britzl/defcon is defcon/). The folder pins the library's own upstream repository and ref once — an authored library is the sole maintainer of its namespace, so it carries its own repo/ref rather than the shared vendored commit: | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | ------ | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | repo | yes | The GitHub or Codeberg repository URL, e.g. https://github.com/britzl/defcon. upstream:library-check reads no other host. | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | license | no | SPDX-style license id, surfaced by the library page's provenance block. Defaults to "". | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | --------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | library.json | refKind | no | "tag" or "commit" when upstream publishes no stable release (GitHub's latest release skips prereleases), so the docs page's adopt step names the pinned archive instead of linking a releases page. Omit it for a repo with releases. | | File | Field | Required | What it is | | --------------- | ----- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | reviewed.json | ref | yes | The immutable upstream ref to pin. Prefer the newest stable release tag (git ls-remote --tags <repo>) — never invent one. When upstream publishes no tags, pin the current default-branch commit SHA instead; the docs page renders the full SHA as the source ref. | Each forked module is one entry in library.json's forks list: | Field | Required | What it is | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | authored | yes | Path of the vendored authored/forked .d.ts, relative to the library folder — fork/<moduleId>.d.ts. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | moduleId | yes | The library's runtime require path, dotted (e.g. defcon.console). This is the declare module name inside the vendored .d.ts. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ----------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | namespace | yes | The artifact stem — the emitted file is api-doc/<namespace>.json. Either a bare stem (defcon) or the dotted moduleId (orthographic.camera): fork onto the retired module name when it already equals the publish namespace, and reach for a bare stem only when nothing else owns it. The orthographic.camera worked example below settles the choice. | | Field | Required | What it is | | -------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | apiDoc | yes | The site's model output path (api-doc/<namespace>.json). | | Field | Required | What it is | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | fidelity | no | Defaults to fidelity/<namespace>.json. A fork records no fidelity artifact (see below); the field mirrors the sibling lanes for a future hand-authored target that wants one. | | Field | Required | What it is | | ------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | upstreamLua | one of two | Library-folder-relative paths of the vendored upstream .lua this target's surface is measured against. See surface parity. | | Field | Required | What it is | | --------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | parityVerdict | one of two | Why this target vendors no upstream .lua: { "reason": ..., "note": ... }. Mutually exclusive with upstreamLua. | | Field | Required | What it is | | -------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | instanceType | when upstream has methods | The exported interface the fork declares the module's instances with, e.g. BehaviorTree. Required once the vendored upstream defines a function M:name(…) method, which parity measures against that interface's methods; it needs upstreamLua. See surface parity. | A missing required field fails loudly, naming the field, the offending entry and its library.json. So does a folder named other than its repository, a folder without reviewed.json, and a module another library folder already names. upstreamLua and parityVerdict are individually optional but jointly mandatory: every entry declares exactly one. Neither field is in the required list, yet an entry declaring neither — or both — fails the same way, naming the offender. That is deliberate. A target with no declaration would otherwise sit in the config indistinguishable from a measured-and-clean one, so the config cannot express "nobody has looked at this yet"; you either measure the surface or record why you cannot.

subsoap / defsave defsave Save and load config and user data persistently between a Defold project's sessions

subsoap/defmath (a pure-Lua math-helper module) is a third fork with the same reference-entry shape, illustrating the no-tag case: upstream publishes no git tags, so ref pins the default-branch commit SHA (c67c227322334056cea7a631f3ddcdf2bcfd480c) rather than a semver tag. The defmath page attributes to that SHA and its sourceUrl points at .../tree/c67c2273… — expected, not a defect. Its surface also references core engine types: upstream writes them as vmath.vector3 | vmath.vector4 / vmath.quaternion, but the fork — like every vendored declaration in this package — carries the core-type-renamed ambient Vector3 | Vector4 / Quaternion. These resolve in library check, which compiles every fork against the engine types the CLI ships, so a fork consuming engine types needs no special wiring.

subsoap/defsave (a save/load helper, pinned to the v1.2.6 tag) is the first fork to correct a surface rather than re-home it: the ts-defold binding declared 7 of upstream's 14 functions and just one of its 16 config fields (appname), and three of the seven returned the wrong type. Neither pure option fits — keep fails the cost model (upstream is frozen and the surface is tiny) and a fork alone would knowingly re-home a half-missing surface, while a full hand-author would rewrite five declarations that are already right (four correct functions plus appname). So fork first, then hand-correct against the pin: copy the retired .d.ts, add the missing members, and fix the wrong signatures reading upstream's Lua as the authority. Extending a fork is gate-safe: the identity diff compares the printed declaration to the vendored fixture, not to the retired ts-defold surface. But that diff proves emission fidelity only — the print loses nothing relative to the vendored .d.ts; it does not check the vendored surface against upstream. That accuracy rests on the manual audit against defsave.lua at the pin plus the per-library shape assertions in packages/cli/src/library/sync-authored-types.test.ts, so correcting a fork moves the accuracy burden onto the author, not onto a gate. Narrowing a wrong return is a breaking change for consumers and belongs in the changelog's ### Breaking section; a types package's value is accuracy, so do not keep a declaration you can see is wrong. Two limits are worth knowing before you correct a surface. Upstream Lua that falls off the end of a function returns nil, so a predicate like defsave's key_exists is boolean | undefined, not boolean — read every branch, not just the explicit returns. And a module's export let fields are still read-only through a consumer's import as ns, so a compile proof pins their types by reading them; there is no way to prove assignability through a namespace import.

The corpus pin and a consumer's declared dependency are different things, and conflating them is the first mistake a repo-wide find-and-replace makes. Several CLI tests hardcode archive URLs and extracted-entry paths, and some of them pin exactly the corpus string. packages/cli/src/library-match.test.ts, packages/cli/src/resolve.test.ts and packages/cli/src/druid-resolve-e2e.test.ts all carry a druid version literal in consumer archive URLs, and it can equal the ref the registry entry holds. That collision is the reason a repo-wide find-and-replace is unsafe: one copy of the version must move with the bump (the registry entry, and the provenance assertions named above), and another must not. normalizeSourceId (packages/cli/src/library-match.ts) strips /archive/<ref>.zip and matches on the repo name alone, so a consumer fixture is version-independent either way — which cuts both ways. Rewriting its version leaves the suite green, so a green bun test is not evidence the rewrite was correct. The 1.2.3 fixtures in packages/cli/src/library-scene-materialize.test.ts and the later resolve.test.ts cases are consumer fixtures on the same footing and equally out of scope. Leave them alone. A corpus bump changes the data folder, the floors, the emitted artifacts and the docs indexes. It does not change what a test project declares in its game.project.
The couplings a re-pin moves with it
The decision: fork, hand-author, or keep?

The druid entry is the reference shape: sourceGlobs snapshots the whole druid/ tree; ignore drops its tests and examples; moduleId druid.druid scopes the exported functions to druid/druid.lua while the interfaces merge from every file; typeRenames maps druid's vmath references onto the toolchain's branded Vector types; externalTypes hands druid's callback fields to the event library that owns them. From these fixtures, or from the druid archive a project depends on, resolve prints the declaration it materializes into a consuming project as druid.druid.

The generated lanes report a coverage number because a parse can lose type information the original had. An authored .d.ts cannot: the printed declaration is the vendored source plus doc comments, so the go/no-go gate is a forked-vs-printed identity diff on types — what resolve prints, with its comments removed, is identical to the vendored fork/<moduleId>.d.ts with its comments removed. sync-authored-types.test.ts asserts this for every fork, and print-library.test.ts checks the lane dispatch serves that print. No fidelity/ artifact is written. Read that gate narrowly. It proves emission fidelity — both sides of the diff are the toolchain repo's own files, so all it certifies is that the print loses no type relative to the vendored .d.ts. It says nothing about whether the vendored surface matches upstream, and there is no primary source to measure it against — that is what "no structured type source" means. A verbatim fork inherits whatever accuracy the binding it copied already had; a corrected fork (see defsave below) is only as accurate as the manual audit behind it. So pin the corrections with per-library shape assertions in packages/cli/src/library/sync-authored-types.test.ts — the closest thing this lane has to an upstream check.

The Library update workflow (the toolchain's .github/workflows/library-update.yml) runs library update over packages/library-types/data/ with the latest CLI, then opens one pull request per library it wrote, from the branch library-update/<library>. It runs daily, and when dispatched: A PR that moves a pin is titled update <library> to <ref>; one that only adds commits to a review is titled record <library> commits. A later run force-pushes the same branch and retitles its open PR, so a library never has two. A library that cannot be read upstream is named in the run's log, and fails the run once every other library has its PR. A run dispatched while another is going waits for it to finish.

The library update workflow runs daily, so a library that moved upstream gets one PR from library-update/<library>, refreshed on each run. The bot closes that PR, with a comment, once a run finds the library current or held, or no longer lists the library, as when a new data folder renames it. The bot files an issue titled library update cannot land <library> only when it cannot land a library: library update failed for it, or its PR's checks were red when the run started. The issue names the failure or links the PR, a later run edits it rather than filing a second, and the bot closes it, with a comment, once neither holds. A run reads the checks before it refreshes any PR, so an issue opens or closes up to one run after the checks finish. bun run upstream:library-check is a manual report that no workflow runs. It scans all five registries and reports, per upstream repo, whether the pin has fallen behind: Three things about the report are worth knowing before you act on it: The unit of work is the repo, not the module. britzl/defold-input backs ten authored modules and britzl/defold-orthographic is consumed by two lanes. One bump answers every dependent, so the check groups by repo + ref, counts the dependents, and lists them under --json. A commit-pinned repo is only actionable when the delta touches a path this repo reads. The registries already record which upstream files each target consumes, so a README-only commit on a pinned repo's default branch reports as behind-head without asking you to do anything. A pin that feeds only the fidelity comparison is marked internal. When every dependent is a markdown or OpenAPI target whose decision is not go, no user receives its output, so the report sets internal and the prose line ends in (internal); the bump needs no changelog bullet. It is still actionable: a stale spec hides upstream movement from the go/no-go comparison. The library update bot does not update these targets, so this report is the only place their drift shows. A repo the check could not read at all is reported as unknown and exits the command non-zero. That is deliberate: a renamed or deleted upstream must not look like "current". The check reads GitHub and Codeberg; a repo on any other host reports unknown. When an upstream moves, search the author's old repos for a pointer to the new home before withdrawing the library. Re-pointing means a new repo and a new ref together, because a moved repo often has rewritten history and the old commit no longer exists there.

The PR body names the change and the members upstream added, removed and changed. A changed PR whose three lists are all empty had no single review of the pinned commit to compare with, so read the diff under source/ instead. The library-check run on the PR says whether the library still fits: a module below its floor is named with the value it measured, and a usage/ proof that stops compiling is named by file and line. Fix the fork, floor or proof as the couplings a re-pin moves with it describe, on a branch of your own: the next run force-pushes library-update/<library> and drops any commit pushed to it. Once yours merges, the next run finds the library current and closes the bot's PR.

The previous section holds for types: upstream ships none, so there is nothing to measure a fork's type annotations against. It does not hold for the surface. Upstream Lua declares its member names and its parameter names in plain source, and those are comparable — a fork that never got a member, or that dropped a trailing parameter, is measurable without any type information at all.

The registries only see libraries someone already added. <data folder>/asset-portal.json records every Defold Asset Portal entry, pinned to a defold/asset-portal commit, with the GitHub repo each entry names classified by what a dependency on it installs: The sync refuses to start without GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, because it makes about five API calls per entry. It follows renames, so repo is the canonical URL (the portal's britzl/extension-imgui is recorded as defold/extension-imgui). Each repo is read at its latest release, else its newest tag, else its default-branch head. Files count only inside the repo's game.project [library] include_dirs, since nothing else reaches a project that adds the dependency. Each entry's kind is the first row that matches: | kind | The repo at its pin | | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | no-source | is not readable on GitHub; reason is no-github-url or not-found | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | not-a-dependency | declares no include_dirs: a tool, sample or editor integration | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- | | script-api | ships a .script_api, which resolve already types | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | | native-untyped | ships an ext.manifest without a .script_api | | kind | The repo at its pin | | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | pure-lua-annotated | ships Lua, and one of up to four sampled files carries ---@ annotations | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ---------- | ---------------------------------- | | pure-lua | ships Lua with no annotated sample | | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | no-lua-api | ships no Lua: shaders, materials, sounds or editor scripts only | bun run asset-portal:report joins the manifest against every lane registry and the defold org listing in defold-extensions.json, offline, and prints four answers: Tracked: entries whose repo a registry already pins, counted per lane. The portal lane counts the script-api entries that have reference pages. A tracked entry files here whatever its kind. Candidates: untracked entries of kind script-api, native-untyped, pure-lua-annotated or pure-lua that are not archived, not a fork, were pushed within 730 days of the sync, and carry no verdict. They are grouped by kind and ranked by stars, which only order the list and say nothing about quality. Declined: untracked entries with a recorded verdict, each with its reason. Nothing to type: untracked no-lua-api, not-a-dependency and no-source entries. A line between them counts the untracked entries with a Lua API that fail the maintenance rule. After a manifest sync, give every script-api candidate its reference pages: It converts each .script_api under the entry's include_dirs at the pin asset-portal.json recorded, writes the page list to <data folder>/asset-portal-script-api.json and one doc per page under asset-portal-script-api/api-doc/, and rebuilds that directory on every run. Those entries then count as tracked on the portal lane. A doc that fails to convert, a page key another page already holds, or a page key that is not one safe route and file name (ASCII letters, digits, , . and -, starting and ending with a letter, digit or , and not a Windows device name such as CON or NUL before its first .) stops the sync before it changes any file, instead of dropping the page. A page key names only the page's api-doc file: its address comes from the library's origin repo, as Library page addresses describes. A library that moved forge keeps a stale portal entry: the portal's Klaleus/library-defold-checkpoint is gone from GitHub, and the authored lane pins codeberg.org/Klaleus/defold-checkpoint. Map such an entry to the tracked repo in packages/library-types/asset-portal-aliases.json. The report refuses to run when an alias names an entry the manifest no longer lists, or a repo no registry pins. An entry whose pinned tree holds no runtime module a project would require, such as an editor script, an import tool or a project template, stays a candidate until someone looks. Record the decision in packages/library-types/asset-portal-verdicts.json: a map from entry id to one short reason naming what the tree holds instead. A verdict takes the entry off the candidate list for good, whatever its maintenance state. The report refuses to run when a verdict names an entry the manifest no longer lists, or an entry a registry pins directly or through an alias, since either verdict is stale. The weekly Library upstream check workflow (the toolchain's .github/workflows/library-upstream-check.yml) compares the portal head's entry ids with the manifest. When ids were added or removed, it opens one issue, titled Asset portal entries differ from asset-portal.json, that lists them and names the re-sync command. The title never changes, so later runs stay quiet while that issue is open. A changed entry under an unchanged id is not reported, because the portal rewrites release metadata every six hours.

The upstream path is derived from moduleId: replace the dots with slashes and append .lua, so in.button is in/button.lua and richtext.richtext is richtext/richtext.lua. Fetch that path at the library's pinned ref and vendor it under the library folder's source/upstream/, at the same path it has upstream — so britzl/defold-input at in/button.lua lands at defold-input/source/upstream/in/button.lua. Vendor only the module file the target names, never the whole repository: the parity report measures only the files the target names, so any other copy is dead weight. The reader accepts two closing forms: a bare return M, and a callable module's return setmetatable(M, { … }) — on one line or spread over several, as long as it starts at column 0. It refuses a metatable carrying index, and one named by a variable whose keys it cannot see, in both cases throwing rather than parsing. A delegated member never appears at column 0, so parsing anyway would report a short surface as the whole one and raise the target's coverage for it. An indented return setmetatable(instance, { … }) inside a factory function is not the module's close and is ignored, which is what the column-0 rule buys. The reader also reads the entries of the returned table's constructor: a column-0 local M = { whose entries run over the following lines gives each top-level name = value entry as a member, a function(…) value as a callable one, so this constructor counts Client as M.Client = Client would: A constructor that closes on its opening line, local M = { NAME = "admob" }, is read too. A nested table's keys stay out. An entry it cannot name — a bracketed ["key"] or a positional value — or entries written on an opening line whose constructor continues past it throw, for the same reason a delegating metatable does. A class module's column-0 function M:name(…) methods are read as well, each with its named parameters and without the implicit self. Parity keys them <instanceType>:<name> and compares them with the methods of the interface the entry names as its instanceType, so a missing or short method costs callable coverage like any other member. The self-index M.index = M that makes the module a class adds no member. A column-0 colon method on any other table throws, since its instances are reached through nothing the reader sees, and so does a name defined both as a method and as a . member. List the vendored paths in upstreamLua, then regenerate: That writes fidelity/authored/<namespace>.json per measured target. Both halves of the upstream surface are compared, on two axes reported side by side. The declared side of each is the fork's api-doc/<namespace>.json — the surface the /api page renders, so the report measures what a reader actually sees. Only the fork's own members are compared. An api-doc element marked global: true is a file-scope name the library installs into the environment, defined upstream in files the target does not vendor, so it is a member of no module and enters neither axis — calling one a phantom would describe real upstream API as invented. declaredGlobals records how many were set aside: 30 for deftest, whose telescope assertions are ambient, and 87 for boom, which declares one module member beside its whole ambient game API. The callable axis, upstream members carrying a parameter list against api-doc FUNCTION elements: | Field | What it counts | | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | upstreamMembers | Callable members the upstream module defines. | | Field | What it counts | | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | declaredGlobals | Declared names the fork installs into the environment rather than onto the module. Counted, never compared. | | Field | What it counts | | ----------------- | ---------------------------- | | declaredMembers | Functions the fork declares. | | Field | What it counts | | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | missingMembers | Upstream members the fork does not declare at all. | | Field | What it counts | | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | phantomMembers | Declared members upstream does not have. | | Field | What it counts | | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | arityMismatches | Shared names whose parameter counts disagree, each with both numbers — the fork's being the widest signature it declares. Names are not compared — a fork may rename parameters freely. | | Field | What it counts | | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | undocumentedMembers | Upstream prose that reached neither the fork nor the import — a member whose accepted block carries no summary to lower, being nothing but tags or nothing but the member's own name. | | Field | What it counts | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | importedDocs | Declared elements carrying upstream's own doc, its summary or only its parameter and return docs, because the fork supplied none or did not pin its own. Counted on both axes. | | Field | What it counts | | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | refusedDocBlocks | Refused upstream blocks the fork left unanswered — neither documented in the fork's own words nor excused by a recorded parityException. Counted on both axes, and the one term that reports prose the import never saw. Authoring the brief clears the charge. | | Field | What it counts | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | refusedDocBlocksTotal | The raw refusal count, before the answered and excused ones are subtracted. Kept so a refusedDocBlocks of 0 cannot be misread as upstream writing no ---only blocks. | | Field | What it counts | | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | variadicMembers | Shared members compared against a floor rather than an exact count, upstream being variadic. | | Field | What it counts | | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | overloadedMembers | Shared members the fork declares as several overloads, so the comparison had a set of counts to accept rather than one. | | Field | What it counts | | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | placeholderMembers | Shared members whose upstream definition ends in a bare with no ... after it, dropped before the counts were compared. | | Field | What it counts | | ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | callableCoverage | Fraction of upstream members that are declared and agree on arity. | An upstream definition ending in ... has no fixed parameter count to disagree with, so function M.play(...) is compared against its named parameters as a floor: the fork must declare at least them, and anything beyond is the rest. variadicMembers says how many shared members that weaker check covered, so a callableCoverage of 1 over a variadic surface cannot be read as fully verified. A fork may also declare one name as several overloads, modelling an upstream body that branches on whether an argument was passed — monarch.transitions.gui.create declares create(node) and create() against upstream's single M.create(node) and its if node then branch. That is a set of call shapes, and the member agrees when any one of them meets the rule above; reading a single count would charge a correct fork for whichever overload the api-doc happened to list last. A disagreement is still reported as one number, the widest shape the fork offers. overloadedMembers counts every member compared that way, for the same reason variadicMembers exists: agreeing because one shape matched is a weaker result than agreeing outright. A generated module can also end a definition in a bare that no body reads and no doc comment describes — nakama.lua opens "Code generated by codegen/generate-rest.go" and 66 of its exports end that way. A trailing discard is not a parameter a consumer can pass meaningfully, so charging the fork for omitting it would report the instrument's defect as the fork's. It is dropped before the counts are compared, and only when it is last: a upstream names in the middle still has to be passed for the parameters after it to land. A written before a ... tail is last only in appearance — a caller fills that slot for any vararg to land — so it is still charged. placeholderMembers counts every member the drop covered, whether or not it changed the verdict. The drop is not merely subtractive — a fork that declared the discard as a real parameter disagrees once it is gone, which is how create_protobuf_any was found declaring a second parameter upstream does not take. The field axis, upstream constants (M.SOME_CONSTANT = "X") against api-doc VARIABLE elements. A TYPEDEF is a type rather than a runtime member and enters neither axis: | Field | What it counts | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | upstreamFields | Non-callable members the upstream module defines. | | Field | What it counts | | ---------------- | --------------------------------------- | | declaredFields | Non-callable members the fork declares. | | Field | What it counts | | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | missingFields | Upstream constants the fork does not declare — values its users cannot reach. | | Field | What it counts | | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | phantomFields | Declared constants upstream has in neither half — names the fork invented. | | Field | What it counts | | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | | fieldCoverage | Fraction of upstream fields the fork declares. | A name that is callable on either side belongs to the callable axis and is never also counted as a field, so one defect is never charged twice. A fork that declared an upstream function as a constant of a callable type would otherwise be charged on both axes at once — once as a missing member, once as a phantom field — and the second charge would describe an upstream name as invented. No measured target produces the shape today, the one that did having since been corrected, so the rule stands on the classifier rather than on any corpus case. floors in the library's library.json ratchets both axes per module, keyed by moduleId as { "callable": 1, "field": 1 }, each against its own floor: either may rise, neither may fall. A regeneration that lowers either number reds the gate, a floor entry that names only one axis is rejected when the library is read rather than leaving the other unratcheted, and library check measures the fork against the same floors. A non-empty missingMembers, phantomMembers, arityMismatches, missingFields, or phantomFields is a correction to make in the fork — never a number to re-baseline. The measurement exists so the gap stays visible while it is being closed; the current numbers are the honest starting point, not a target. The committed reports are held to a fresh measurement for the same reason: authored-parity-floor.test.ts re-measures every target and reds when a committed report differs, so a re-vendor, fork edit or reader change that moves a number reds until bun run --cwd packages/library-types parity rewrites the reports and the coverage change is reviewed. nakama is the worked example and the rollout's closing statement: its fork declared 166 functions against upstream's 156 with only 4 agreeing on arity — the corpus's worst case, and the last target to reach a full callableCoverage. Closing it took every kind of correction this page describes. Requests upstream had flattened into positional parameters were still declared as a body table, so a caller following the fork passed a table where upstream reads a string. 84 exports ended in retry_policy, cancellation_token the fork declared nowhere, and the two types that pair with them — cancel and cancellation_token — were themselves among the 16 members it never declared. 26 declared names were not on this module at all, the realtime socket surface among them: the pinned nakama.lua requires that module privately and exposes it only through create_socket. Eleven of the 26 have a counterpart on nakama.socket, now vendored as a target of its own; the other fifteen — thirteen message constructors, a stream-presence listener and a request constructor upstream no longer generates — match neither module at the pin and were phantoms on an older nakama-defold. The field axis then closed on the same terms: all 12 of upstream's enum constants are declared, so both axes read 1. boom is the opposite shape: it declares one of the six members boom/boom.lua defines, the other five being the final/init/on_input/ on_message/update lifecycle hooks boom.script calls rather than API a user writes. Those five are justified rather than missing — see below — so the target reports callableCoverage: 1 with no fork edit at all. Read that beside declaredGlobals: nearly the whole library reaches its users as ambient globals, which this axis does not measure.

The workflow turns on auto-merge, so the PR merges once ci-done passes, only when both hold: the change is kept or added, or the PR only records commits; every file the PR touches is the library's reviewed.json or under its source/, and CI scopes it as library data. The second is read from the commit, not from what library update reported, so a file anything else wrote keeps the PR for a human. Every other PR stays open. A run turns off an open PR's auto-merge before it replaces the branch, and turns it on again only for the commit it read.

Two facts decide it: It is plain Lua (installed via Defold's Fetch Libraries, no .script_api), and its source carries inline ---@ annotations — ---@class, ---@field, ---@param, ---@return on the public module. A hand-written library with no annotations is not a LuaLS target; those are maintained as hand-vendored .d.ts forks. A library whose annotations are sparse (near-zero fidelity coverage, see below) will emit a hollow surface and is not worth adding. The library's runtime require path (its moduleId) must not already be claimed by another library in library data — two front-ends emitting the same module would collide.

ump.request_consent_info_update(test_device: boolean, test_device_hashed_id: string, callback?: function, defer_form?: boolean) Request fresh consent information and show a consent form if required. Call on every launch. The callback runs on the Defold update thread after the update and any required form finish unless defer_form is true. In deferred mode the callback runs after the information update, before any form opens; call show_consent_form_if_required to finish the flow. Pass an empty string when test_device is false. callback — Called when the update and any required form finish. defer_form — Pause after the information update so an application notice can precede a required form. Defaults to false.
ump.REQUEST_STATE_COMPLETE 1; update and form step finished without a UMP error.

wavedash.EVENT_PURCHASE_COMPLETED Fired once per purchase made while the game is running (in-game paywall, game page, gift, another tab), plus, at launch, once per consumable still unfulfilled. Payload: { purchaseId, contentIdentifier, type, fulfilled, purchasedAt, receiptJwt }. Durables arrive with fulfilled true, already granted. For a consumable, grant it, then call fulfill_purchase_async(purchaseId); until then it's redelivered every launch, so dedupe on purchaseId if you persist grants.

wavedash.fulfill_purchase_async(purchase_id: string): function Mark a consumable purchase fulfilled once the grant is saved, so it stops being redelivered. A game's backend can do the same with POST /api/purchases/{purchaseId}/fulfill and the purchase's receiptJwt; both are idempotent, so calling either or both is safe. Resolves with a status in data: FULFILLED, ALREADY_FULFILLED (also success), or NOT_FOUND (unknown or refunded: don't grant it). This is an asynchronous function. The result will be delivered as an event with id 'fulfillPurchase' or as a return value if the function is called from a coroutine. response — Returns { status } in data. (Note: Only if called from within a coroutine)
wavedash.FULFILL_PURCHASE_STATUS_ALREADY_FULFILLED fulfill_purchase_async status: also success. The game or its backend fulfilled it earlier, or it's a durable.
wavedash.FULFILL_PURCHASE_STATUS_FULFILLED fulfill_purchase_async status: marked fulfilled by this call.

whiteboxdev / library-defold-rendy rendy A versatile camera suite and render pipeline

whiteboxdev/library-defold-persist (a save/load helper, pinned to the b37f6104… commit SHA since upstream publishes no tags) is the first fork to arrive here from a markdown no-go rather than from having no documented source at all. Its README documents all six functions by name but no parameters and no returns, so the markdown gate scored signature-loss and refused the cutover. That verdict retired the README as a regeneration path — and nothing more. Running the cost model on the still-open maintenance question gives fork: the ts-defold surface is five fully-typed functions in 34 lines, upstream is abandoned (its README redirects to a successor project) so the surface cannot churn, and the recorded loss was the README's, not the .d.ts's. So the cutover itself was verbatim — the identity diff made fidelity 100% by construction, and it shipped no type change at all. The later and separately-auditable edit that anticipated has since landed: the fork now also declares exists, the sixth function upstream's Lua defines and ts-defold never had. Severing does not erase the markdown verdict. persist's no-go/signature-loss record and its README snapshot stay exactly as recorded, and the gate still re-derives the decision on every run — it just compares against the vendored fork instead of the deleted fixtures/ts-defold/ snapshot. That is sound because the comparison is re-derived against whatever the fork now declares, not against an identity: adding exists moved two name-set terms and left the no-go/signature-loss decision exactly where it was. Keeping a dead library-targets.json row alive to feed that lookup would have been the wrong fix: it would make the file stop meaning still ts-defold-sourced, which is the signal the remaining Bucket-C libraries are measured against.

For numbers, pass (value, min, max) and returns the clamped number. For vectors, pass (v_in_place, value, min, max) to modify v_in_place. min and max can be numbers or matching vector types. value_or_out — For numbers, the value to clamp. xmath.lerp(t_or_out: number | vector3 | vector4 | quaternion, n1_or_t: number | vector3 | vector4 | quaternion, n2_or_v1: number | vector3 | vector4 | quaternion, v2: vector3 | vector4 | quaternion): number Linearly interpolate between two numbers, vectors, or quaternions. For numbers, pass (t, n1, n2) and returns the interpolated number. For vectors/quaternions, pass (v_in_place, t, v1, v2) to modify v_in_place. t_or_out — For numbers, the interpolation factor. For vectors/quaternions, the output value to store the result. n1_or_t — For numbers, the start value. For vectors/quaternions, the interpolation factor. n2_or_v1 — For numbers, the end value. For vectors/quaternions, the start value. v2 — For vectors/quaternions only, the end value. result — For number inputs, returns the interpolated number. For vector/quaternion inputs, modifies v_in_place and returns nothing.

xoshiro256.clone(state: userdata, out?: userdata): userdata Creates and returns an independent copy of the state
xoshiro256.float_range(state: userdata, m: number, n: number): number Generates a random number in floating range [m, n)
xoshiro256.from_string(serialized_state: string): userdata Convert previously saved string back to state.

xoshiro256.random(state: userdata, m?: number, n?: number): number When called without arguments, returns a uniform pseudo-random real number in the range [0,1). When called with an integer number m, returns a uniform pseudo-random integer in the range [1, m]. When called with two integer numbers m and n, returns a uniform pseudo-random integer in the range [m, n].

xoshiro256.seed(seed: number | string): userdata Create state for the pseudo-random generator: equal seeds produce equal sequences of numbers. Accepts a number or a string (decimal representation of uint64, max 20 digits in the string) if full 64-bit precision required. State is seeded using splitmix64 algorithm.
xoshiro256.to_string(state: userdata): string Convert state to string. Used for saving the state. String is formed as 4 uint64 values separated by ':', e.g. "s0:s1:s2:s3".
